docs.title: cliffy
docs.text:
Describe a command-line tool in YAML. Get a real Python CLI.

cliffy reads a manifest that lists your commands, their parameters and the code each one runs, and generates a Typer application from it. Command bodies are plain Python, and any line that starts with $ runs as a shell command, so a manifest can replace a folder of one-off scripts with a single CLI that has help text, typed arguments and subcommands.

docs.title: A CLI in 60 seconds
docs.text:
1. Install cliffy (Python 3.11 to 3.15):

$ pip install cliffy

2. Write a manifest and save it as hello.yaml:

hello.yaml
name: hello
version: 0.1.0
help: Hello world!

commands:
  shell: $ echo "hello from shell"
  python: print("hello from python")
  greet:
    help: Greet someone by name
    params:
      - name: str!
      - --shout|-s: bool = False
    run: |
      message = f"Hello, {name}!"
      print(message.upper() if shout else message)

tests:
  - shell: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - python: assert result.output == "hello from python\n"
  - greet Ada: assert result.output == "Hello, Ada!\n"
  - greet Ada --shout: assert "HELLO, ADA!" in result.output

3. Load it. cliffy generates the CLI and puts a hello command into your Python environment:

$ cli load hello.yaml
✨ Generated hello CLI v0.1.0 ✨
$ hello -h

4. Use it like any other command:

$ hello shell
hello from shell
$ hello greet Ada --shout
HELLO, ADA!
$ hello --help

 Usage: hello [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 Hello world!

╭─ Options ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --version                                                                  │
│ --install-completion          Install completion for the current shell.    │
│ --show-completion             Show completion for the current shell, to    │
│                               copy it or customize the installation.       │
│ --help                -h      Show this message and exit.                  │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Commands ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ shell                                                                      │
│ python                                                                     │
│ greet   Greet someone by name                                              │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The tests section at the bottom of the manifest is optional. cli test hello.yaml runs it.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Python and shell in one place. Run scripts are Python; lines starting with $ become subprocess calls. See Shell commands.
  • Typed parameters with a short syntax. name: str! is a required argument and --count|-c: int = 1 is an option. See Params and types.
  • Groups, aliases and templates. db.create nests a command, delete|rm adds an alias and command templates share params between commands. See Commands, groups and aliases.
  • A fast edit loop. cli dev reloads the CLI every time you save the manifest. See Hot-reload dev loop.
  • Tests next to the commands. cli test runs the assertions you keep in the manifest. See Testing manifests.
  • One file to ship. cli build packs the CLI and its dependencies into a single executable zipapp, a single Python script or a native executable. See Building executables.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
manifest.yaml ──► validate ──► generate Python (Typer or Click) ──► load │ run │ build
  1. cliffy renders the manifest with Jinja2, parses the YAML and validates it against the manifest schema.
  2. It generates one Python module. cli render prints that module, so nothing about the result is hidden.
  3. cli load installs the module as a command, cli run executes it once and cli build packages it.

docs.title: AI commands
docs.text:
Cliffy includes AI-powered commands that generate manifests and answer questions about cliffy. They live in the cli ai command group; every option is listed in the CLI reference.

The AI commands are a convenience. Nothing else in cliffy needs a model: a manifest written by hand, or by an agent from the manifest schema, works the same way.

Note

Requires the ai extra: pip install "cliffy[ai]". See Installation. Without it, cli ai commands exit with an install hint; the rest of cliffy is unaffected.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
The AI commands are built on Pydantic AI and work with any model it supports. Models are named provider:model, and each provider reads its API key from its usual environment variable.

The model is picked in this order:

  1. the --model / -m option
  2. the CLIFFY_AI_MODEL environment variable

  3. a default for the first provider that has an API key set:

    API key Default model GOOGLE_API_KEY (or GEMINI_API_KEY) google:gemini-flash-latest ANTHROPIC_API_KEY anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5 OPENAI_API_KEY openai:gpt-5.4-mini 
# use the default model of the provider whose key is set
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='your-api-key'
cli ai generate mycli "Create a todo app"

# pick a model for one command
cli ai generate mycli "Create a todo app" --model openai:gpt-5.5

# or for the whole shell session
export CLIFFY_AI_MODEL=google:gemini-2.5-pro

Tip

Use --preview to print the fully constructed prompt instead of sending it. This needs neither a model nor an API key.

docs.title: Generating a manifest
docs.text:
Generate complete CLI manifests from natural language descriptions:

cli ai generate mycli "Create a CLI for managing docker containers with commands to list, start, stop and remove containers"
cli load mycli.yaml

The model's reply is validated before anything is written: it has to be valid YAML, match the manifest schema, and produce a CLI that is valid Python. A reply that fails is sent back to the model together with the reason, up to --retries times (default 2). If no valid manifest comes back, the command fails and writes nothing.

mycli.yaml is written to the current directory, or to --output-dir. An existing file is only replaced with --force.

Warning

Validation checks that the manifest loads, not that the commands do what you asked. Read the generated run blocks before running the CLI.

docs.title: Asking questions
docs.text:
Get AI assistance for understanding and working with cliffy:

cli ai ask "How do I create nested subcommands?"

The question is answered from a reference built from your installed cliffy version: its command list, the annotated cli init template and the manifest JSON schema.

You can also get targeted help about specific CLIs by referencing a manifest or a loaded CLI:

cli ai ask --cli mycli.yaml "How do I add input validation to the start command?"

The answer is printed to stdout and token usage to stderr, so the answer can be redirected to a file.

docs.title: Giving cliffy's documentation to an agent
docs.text:
cli ai llms-txt prints cliffy's documentation as a single text file in the llms.txt layout: the quickstart, the guides and the CLI and manifest references.

cli ai llms-txt > cliffy-llms.txt

The file is bundled with the installed package, so it needs no network access, no model and no ai extra, and it always describes the version you have installed. Put it in the context of a coding agent and it can write and fix manifests without looking anything up.

The same file is published with the documentation at /llms.txt.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
A cliffy manifest describes a CLI in cliffy's own vocabulary: commands, params, run. A blueprint lets you bring your own vocabulary instead. You define the YAML schema that fits your domain and tell cliffy how it maps onto a CLI. Files written in that schema then work with cli load, cli run, cli render, cli test, cli dev, cli docs and cli build, which turns them into a single-file executable.

your YAML spec ──▶ Blueprint (validate, to_manifest) ──▶ cliffy manifest ──▶ Typer or Click code ──▶ one executable file

docs.title: Writing a blueprint
docs.text:
A blueprint is a pydantic model with one required method. The fields are your schema, and to_manifest returns the cliffy manifest for a validated file.

tasks.py
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from cliffy.blueprint import Blueprint
from cliffy.manifest import CLIManifest, Command, RunBlock


class Task(BaseModel):
    run: str | list[str] = Field(description="Shell line(s) to run, in order.")
    help: str = Field(default="", description="What the task does, shown in --help.")


class Tasks(Blueprint):
    """Task runner: every entry under `tasks` becomes a command that runs shell lines"""

    name: str = Field(description="Name of the CLI.")
    version: str = Field(default="0.1.0", description="Version of the CLI.")
    help: str = Field(default="", description="Description of the CLI.")
    tasks: dict[str, str | list[str] | Task] = Field(min_length=1, description="Tasks by name.")

    def to_manifest(self) -> CLIManifest:
        commands = {}
        for name, entry in self.tasks.items():
            task = entry if isinstance(entry, Task) else Task(run=entry)
            lines = [task.run] if isinstance(task.run, str) else task.run
            script = "\n".join(f"subprocess.run({line!r}, shell=True, check=True)" for line in lines)
            commands[name] = Command(help=task.help, run=RunBlock(script))

        return CLIManifest(name=self.name, version=self.version, help=self.help, commands=commands)

A file written in that spec names its blueprint with a top-level blueprint: key:

tasks.yaml
blueprint: tasks.py

name: tasks
help: Project tasks

tasks:
  greet: echo "hello from tasks"
  check:
    - echo "linting"
    - echo "testing"
  release:
    help: Check, then tag the release
    run:
      - echo "linting"
      - echo "tagging"

$ cli run tasks.yaml -- greet
hello from tasks

$ cli load tasks.yaml
$ tasks check
linting
testing

to_manifest may return a CLIManifest or a plain mapping that validates as one. Because the result is an ordinary manifest, everything cliffy does with manifests applies: both the Typer and the Click generator (use_click), requires, tests, command aliases, callbacks and so on.

The whole file is rendered with Jinja2 before the blueprint sees it, exactly like a manifest.

docs.title: Selecting a blueprint
docs.text:
Either in the file, or on the command line. The command line wins.

blueprint: tasks.py

cli run jobs.yaml --blueprint tasks.py -- greet

--blueprint / -b is available on load, run, render, build, dev, test, validate and docs. cli update reuses the blueprint a CLI was loaded with, and cli info shows it.

A blueprint reference is one of:

Reference Meaning tasks.py, ./bp/tasks.py:Tasks A Python file. In a YAML file the path is relative to that file; on the command line it is relative to the working directory. Add :ClassName when the file defines several blueprints. mypackage.blueprints:Tasks An importable class. mypackage.blueprints alone works when the module defines exactly one blueprint. tasks A blueprint provided by an installed package (see Sharing blueprints).

Cliffy reports a reference it cannot use and says why: the file or module does not exist, the name is provided by more than one package, the module defines no blueprint or more than one, or the target is not a blueprint.

docs.title: Validation errors
docs.text:
Unknown keys are rejected by default, so typos are caught. Errors are reported against your spec, with the path to the offending key:

$ cli validate server.yaml
~ server.yaml is not a valid MCPTools spec
  tools[0].name: Value error, `serve` is a reserved name (got 'serve')
  tools[1].parameters[0].type: Input should be 'string', 'integer', 'number', 'boolean' or 'array' (got 'strng')
  tols: Extra inputs are not permitted 💔

Use pydantic validators for rules that go beyond types. To accept unknown keys, set model_config = ConfigDict(extra="ignore") on your blueprint.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Three optional hooks run around to_manifest:

pre_validate(raw) ──▶ validation ──▶ to_manifest() ──▶ post_manifest(manifest) ──▶ code generation ──▶ post_codegen(code)
Hook Receives Use it to pre_validate(cls, raw) (classmethod) The YAML mapping, without the blueprint key Accept shorthand forms, set defaults, rename legacy keys post_manifest(self, manifest) The CLIManifest Adjust the manifest, i.e. add commands every CLI of this kind gets post_codegen(self, code) The generated Python source Adjust the generated code, i.e. prepend a license header 
class Tasks(Blueprint):
    ...

    @classmethod
    def pre_validate(cls, raw):
        # allow `jobs:` as an older name for `tasks:`
        if "jobs" in raw:
            raw = {**raw, "tasks": raw.pop("jobs")}
        return raw

    def post_codegen(self, code):
        return "# generated from a Tasks spec, do not edit\n" + code

docs.title: Editor completion
docs.text:
cli blueprint schema prints the JSON schema of a blueprint's spec.

cli blueprint schema tasks.py -o tasks.schema.json

Reference it from your YAML files to get validation and completion from the YAML language server:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=tasks.schema.json
blueprint: tasks.py

Field descriptions (Field(description=...)) show up as hover documentation.

docs.title: Building a single-file executable
docs.text:
cli build applies the blueprint at build time and bundles the generated CLI with its dependencies into one executable zipapp. With --target script or --target native the same file becomes a single Python script or a compiled executable instead; see Building executables.

$ cli build tasks.yaml -o dist
+ tasks built 📦
  dist/tasks (single file, needs Python >=3.10, 1.8 MB)
  run it with: ./dist/tasks

$ ./dist/tasks greet
hello from tasks

The file runs on any machine with a matching Python. It does not need cliffy, the blueprint, pydantic or the YAML file.

  • Dependencies. Whatever the manifest lists under requires is bundled. Let your blueprint set requires for the packages its generated code imports. The CLI framework (typer, or rich-click with use_click) is added automatically, pinned to the version installed next to cliffy unless requires names it.
  • Interpreter. --python / -p sets the shebang, by default /usr/bin/env python3. The build reports which Python versions the bundle supports. A bundle of pure-Python packages runs on every version its packages accept. A bundle with compiled extensions only runs on the Python minor version it was built with, so build with the version you deploy to. Started with an unsupported Python, the executable exits with a message that says so.
  • Reproducible. Building the same input twice with the same package versions gives a byte-identical file.
  • Errors. When a dependency cannot be installed, the build prints pip's reason and writes no file.

On first run the executable unpacks its packages into ~/.shiv (set SHIV_ROOT to change the location).

docs.title: Sharing blueprints
docs.text:
A package can register blueprints under the cliffy.blueprints entry-point group:

pyproject.toml
[project.entry-points."cliffy.blueprints"]
tasks = "mypackage.blueprints:Tasks"

Once the package is installed, the blueprint is available by name:

blueprint: tasks

$ cli blueprints
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Name  ┃ Blueprint                  ┃ Package   ┃ Description                       ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ tasks │ mypackage.blueprints:Tasks │ mypackage │ Task runner: every entry under... │
└───────┴────────────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

cli blueprints is short for cli blueprint list. The description is the first line of the class docstring.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Two worked examples live in examples/blueprints:

  • tasks.py with tasks.yaml: the task runner from this page.
  • mcp_tools.py with text-tools.yaml: an MCP tool server. The spec lists tools with typed parameters and a Python body. The generated CLI has one command per tool, a tools command that prints the tool definitions, and a serve command that speaks MCP over stdio without extra dependencies. cli build examples/blueprints/text-tools.yaml gives a single file you can register as an MCP server.

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text:
Callbacks are a manifest feature that blueprints often need: code that runs before every command of the CLI, or of one command group. They work with both Typer and Click, and the built-in --version and --aliases options stay in place.

callbacks:
  # no `group`: runs before every command, its params become options of the CLI itself
  - params:
      - name: --verbose
        type: bool
        default: false
        short: -v
        help: Print what is about to run
    invoke_without_command: true
    run: |
      ctx.obj = {"verbose": verbose}
      if ctx.invoked_subcommand is None:
          print("no command given, try --help")
      elif verbose:
          print(f"running {ctx.invoked_subcommand}")

  # runs before every command of the `db` group
  - group: db
    run: print("connecting to db")

commands:
  hello: print("hello")
  db.migrate: print("migrating")

$ mycli --verbose db migrate
running db
connecting to db
migrating
Key Meaning run Code to run. The Typer or Click context is available as ctx. group Command group the callback belongs to, i.e. db or db.tables. Leave it out for the CLI itself. params Options given before the command name, in the same syntax as command params. invoke_without_command Also run when no command is given, instead of showing the help.

Several callbacks for the same target run in the order given. A manifest with only callbacks and no commands is valid, which makes a single-purpose CLI.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: cliffy supports Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15 on macOS and Linux.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install cliffy into the virtual environment you want your CLIs to live in.

pipuv 
$ python -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ pip install cliffy

$ uv venv
$ uv pip install cliffy
$ source .venv/bin/activate

Check the install:

$ cli --help

The package provides two identical commands, cli and cliffy. The documentation uses cli.

Why a virtual environment?

cli load writes a launcher for your CLI into the bin directory of the environment cliffy runs in, and packages listed under requires in a manifest are looked up in that same environment. Keeping cliffy, those packages and your loaded CLIs in one environment is the simplest setup.

docs.title: Run without installing
docs.text:
uvx runs cliffy from a cached, isolated environment:

$ uvx cliffy run hello.yaml greet Ada
$ uvx cliffy build hello.yaml -o dist

A CLI loaded this way lives inside that cached environment. Call it through uvx as well:

$ uvx cliffy load hello.yaml
$ uvx --from cliffy hello greet Ada

docs.title: Install as a tool
docs.text:
pipx install cliffy and uv tool install cliffy put cli on your PATH and keep cliffy in its own environment. This works well for cli run, cli test, cli render and cli build.

Two things differ from a virtual environment install:

  • cli load writes the launcher into the tool's private bin directory, which is not on your PATH. Use cli run or cli build, or add that directory to your PATH.
  • Packages a manifest requires must be installed into the tool environment, for example pipx inject cliffy tabulate or uv tool install cliffy --with tabulate.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
Extra Install Adds rich pip install "cliffy[rich]" rich-click. Styled help for the cli command itself, and required for manifests that set use_click: true. ai pip install "cliffy[ai]" pydantic-ai. Enables the cli ai generate and cli ai ask commands.

Install both with pip install "cliffy[rich,ai]".

Rich itself is always installed because Typer depends on it, so the CLIs you generate have styled help output with or without the rich extra.

docs.title: AI commands
docs.text:
With the ai extra installed, cli ai generate writes a manifest from a description and cli ai ask answers questions about cliffy. Models are named in pydantic-ai's provider:model form and need that provider's API key in the environment:

$ export OPENAI_API_KEY=...
$ cli ai generate mycli "a CLI that manages docker containers" --model openai:gpt-4o

Add --preview to print the prompt without calling a model. Model selection, validation of the generated manifest and cli ai ask are covered in AI commands; the options are listed in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
In this tutorial you build notes, a small CLI that stores notes in a JSON file. Along the way you use every core part of a manifest: commands, params, helper functions, groups, aliases, shell commands and tests. It takes about 15 minutes.

You need cliffy installed in an active virtual environment. See Installation.

The finished manifest is at the end of this page.

docs.title: 1. A manifest with one command
docs.text:
Create a file called notes.yaml:

notes.yaml
name: notes
version: 0.1.0
help: Keep short notes in a JSON file

commands:
  add:
    help: Add a note
    params:
      - text: str!
    run: |
      print(f"Added {text}")

tests:
  - add "buy milk": assert result.output == "Added buy milk\n"
  • name is what you will type to run the CLI. version is shown by notes --version.
  • Each key under commands is a command. run holds its Python code.
  • text: str! declares a parameter called text of type str. The ! makes it required. Parameters are ordinary variables inside run.
  • tests is optional. You will come back to it in step 7.

Run the command without installing anything:

$ cli run notes.yaml add "buy milk"
Added buy milk

cli run generates the CLI, runs it once and throws it away. To see the Python it generated, use cli render:

$ cli render notes.yaml

def add(text: str = typer.Argument(...)):
    print(f"Added {text}")


cli.command("add", help="Add a note",)(add)

Your run script became the body of a Typer command function.

docs.title: 2. Store the notes
docs.text:
The CLI needs to read and write a file. Add imports, vars and functions between help and commands:

notes.yaml
imports: |
  import json
  import os
  from collections import Counter
  from pathlib import Path

vars:
  default_file: notes.json

functions:
  - |
    def notes_path() -> Path:
        return Path(os.environ.get("NOTES_FILE", "{{ default_file }}"))
  - |
    def load_notes() -> list[dict]:
        path = notes_path()
        return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else []
  - |
    def save_notes(notes: list[dict]) -> None:
        notes_path().write_text(json.dumps(notes, indent=2))
  • imports is copied to the top of the generated module.
  • functions is a list of helper functions that every command can call.
  • vars defines manifest variables. {{ default_file }} is replaced with notes.json when the manifest is loaded. More in Vars and Jinja.

docs.title: 3. Describe parameters once with types
docs.text:
text: str! is short, but it has no help text. The types section lets you name a full Typer parameter definition and reuse it. Add this after functions:

notes.yaml
types:
  Text: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Text of the note")
  Tag: str = typer.Option("general", "--tag", "-t", help="Tag to file the note under")

Now replace the add command so that it uses those types and saves the note:

notes.yaml
commands:
  add:
    help: Add a note
    params:
      - text: Text
      - tag: Tag
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      notes.append({"text": text, "tag": tag})
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Added note {len(notes)} [{tag}]")

Try it:

$ cli run notes.yaml add "buy milk"
Added note 1 [general]
$ cli run notes.yaml -- add "book flights" --tag travel
Added note 2 [travel]

The -- separator

When the arguments for your CLI include options such as --tag, put -- after the manifest path. Without it, cli run tries to interpret --tag as one of its own options.

docs.title: 4. Add options and an alias
docs.text:
Add a second command under commands:

notes.yaml
  list|ls:
    help: List notes, optionally filtered by tag
    params:
      - --tag|-t: str = ""
    run: |
      for number, note in enumerate(load_notes(), start=1):
          if not tag or note["tag"] == tag:
              print(f"{number}. [{note['tag']}] {note['text']}")
  • The key list|ls creates the command list and the alias ls.
  • --tag|-t: str = "" is an option (the name starts with --) with the short form -t and an empty string as its default.
$ cli run notes.yaml list
1. [general] buy milk
2. [travel] book flights
$ cli run notes.yaml -- ls -t travel
2. [travel] book flights

docs.title: 5. Exit codes and groups
docs.text:
Commands can stop with an error code by raising typer.Exit. Add remove:

notes.yaml
  remove|rm:
    help: Remove a note by its number
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      if not 1 <= number <= len(notes):
          print(f"No note {number}")
          raise typer.Exit(code=1)
      notes.pop(number - 1)
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Removed note {number}")

A dot in a command key creates a group. These two commands are run as notes tags list and notes tags rename. The entry tags, which has help and no run, sets the help text of the group:

notes.yaml
  tags:
    help: Work with tags

  tags.list:
    help: Count notes per tag
    run: |
      for tag, count in sorted(Counter(note["tag"] for note in load_notes()).items()):
          print(f"{tag} ({count})")

  tags.rename:
    help: Rename a tag on every note
    params:
      - old: str!
      - new: str!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      for note in notes:
          if note["tag"] == old:
              note["tag"] = new
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Renamed {old} to {new}")

$ cli run notes.yaml tags list
general (1)
travel (1)
$ cli run notes.yaml tags rename general home
Renamed general to home
$ cli run notes.yaml remove 7
No note 7

docs.title: 6. Call a shell command
docs.text:
A line that starts with $ is run as a shell command. f{...} inserts the value of a Python expression into it:

notes.yaml
  backup:
    help: Copy the notes file next to itself
    run: |
      $ cp f{notes_path()} f{notes_path()}.bak
      print(f"Backed up to {notes_path()}.bak")

$ cli run notes.yaml backup
Backed up to notes.json.bak

More in Shell commands.

docs.title: 7. Test it
docs.text:
Replace the tests section at the end of the file:

notes.yaml
tests:
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak
  - add "buy milk" --tag home: assert result.output == "Added note 1 [home]\n"
  - add "ship release": assert "Added note 2 [general]" in result.output
  - list: |
      assert "1. [home] buy milk" in result.output
      assert "2. [general] ship release" in result.output
  - ls -t home: assert result_text == "1. [home] buy milk"
  - tags rename general work: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - tags list: assert "work (1)" in result.output
  - backup: assert "Backed up" in result.output
  - remove 9: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - rm 1: assert "Removed note 1" in result.output
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak
  • An entry that starts with $ is a shell step. Here it removes leftover files before and after the run.
  • Every other entry maps a command line to Python assertions. result is the outcome of the command, with result.output and result.exit_code. result_text is the output with surrounding whitespace removed.
$ cli test notes.yaml
✨ Invoking tests ✨
...
💚 All tests passed!

More in Testing manifests.

docs.title: 8. Load it as a real command
docs.text:
So far every call went through cli run. Load the manifest to get a notes command:

$ cli load notes.yaml
✨ Generated notes CLI v0.1.0 ✨
$ notes -h
$ notes add --help

 Usage: notes add [OPTIONS] {text}

 Add a note

╭─ Arguments ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ *    text      <str>  Text of the note [required]                          │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Options ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --tag   -t      <str>  Tag to file the note under [default: general]       │
│ --help  -h             Show this message and exit.                         │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

notes stays available in this environment until you run cli remove notes. After you edit the manifest, run cli update notes to regenerate it, or let cli dev do that on every save.

docs.title: 9. Ship it as one file
docs.text:
$ cli build notes.yaml -o dist
+ notes built 📦
  dist/notes (single file, needs Python >=3.10, 1.8 MB)
  run it with: ./dist/notes
$ ./dist/notes --version
notes, 0.1.0

dist/notes is a self-contained zipapp. It runs on any machine with a compatible Python 3 and does not need cliffy. With --target script you get a single Python script instead, and with --target native a compiled executable that does not even need Python. More in Building executables.

docs.title: The finished manifest
docs.text:
notes.yaml
name: notes
version: 0.1.0
help: Keep short notes in a JSON file

imports: |
  import json
  import os
  from collections import Counter
  from pathlib import Path

vars:
  default_file: notes.json

functions:
  - |
    def notes_path() -> Path:
        return Path(os.environ.get("NOTES_FILE", "{{ default_file }}"))
  - |
    def load_notes() -> list[dict]:
        path = notes_path()
        return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else []
  - |
    def save_notes(notes: list[dict]) -> None:
        notes_path().write_text(json.dumps(notes, indent=2))

types:
  Text: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Text of the note")
  Tag: str = typer.Option("general", "--tag", "-t", help="Tag to file the note under")

commands:
  add:
    help: Add a note
    params:
      - text: Text
      - tag: Tag
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      notes.append({"text": text, "tag": tag})
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Added note {len(notes)} [{tag}]")

  list|ls:
    help: List notes, optionally filtered by tag
    params:
      - --tag|-t: str = ""
    run: |
      for number, note in enumerate(load_notes(), start=1):
          if not tag or note["tag"] == tag:
              print(f"{number}. [{note['tag']}] {note['text']}")

  remove|rm:
    help: Remove a note by its number
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      if not 1 <= number <= len(notes):
          print(f"No note {number}")
          raise typer.Exit(code=1)
      notes.pop(number - 1)
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Removed note {number}")

  tags:
    help: Work with tags

  tags.list:
    help: Count notes per tag
    run: |
      for tag, count in sorted(Counter(note["tag"] for note in load_notes()).items()):
          print(f"{tag} ({count})")

  tags.rename:
    help: Rename a tag on every note
    params:
      - old: str!
      - new: str!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      for note in notes:
          if note["tag"] == old:
              note["tag"] = new
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Renamed {old} to {new}")

  backup:
    help: Copy the notes file next to itself
    run: |
      $ cp f{notes_path()} f{notes_path()}.bak
      print(f"Backed up to {notes_path()}.bak")

tests:
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak
  - add "buy milk" --tag home: assert result.output == "Added note 1 [home]\n"
  - add "ship release": assert "Added note 2 [general]" in result.output
  - list: |
      assert "1. [home] buy milk" in result.output
      assert "2. [general] ship release" in result.output
  - ls -t home: assert result_text == "1. [home] buy milk"
  - tags rename general work: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - tags list: assert "work (1)" in result.output
  - backup: assert "Backed up" in result.output
  - remove 9: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - rm 1: assert "Removed note 1" in result.output
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak

examples:
  - command: notes add "buy milk" --tag home
    description: Add a note tagged home.
  - command: notes ls --tag home
    description: Show only the notes tagged home.

The examples section at the end is shown at the end of notes --help and is used by cli docs.

docs.title: Click and Typer backends
docs.text:
cliffy can generate two kinds of code from the same manifest.

Typer (default) Click Enable with nothing use_click: true Generated code uses typer rich_click, or plain click when rich-click is not installed Extra install none none. pip install "cliffy[rich]" adds rich-formatted help Supported manifest features all all, with the differences listed below

Use Typer unless you have a specific reason to generate Click code. Typer is the backend the rest of this documentation describes.

docs.title: The Click backend
docs.text:
click.yaml
name: clicky
version: 0.1.0
help: The same manifest format, rendered with Click
use_click: true

commands:
  hello|hi:
    help: Say hello
    params:
      - name: str!
      - --times: int = 1
    run: |
      for _ in range(times):
          print(f"hello {name}")

  resize:
    help: Explicit params work like in Typer
    params:
      - name: image
        type: str
        required: true
        help: File to resize
      - name: --width
        type: int
        short: -w
        default: 800
        help: Target width
    run: print(image, width)

  tag:
    help: Raw Click decorators
    params:
      - "@click.option('--loud', is_flag=True, help='Shout the tags')"
      - "@click.argument('tags', nargs=-1)"
    run: |
      for tag in tags:
          print(tag.upper() if loud else tag)

  db.migrate:
    help: Groups work the same way
    run: $ echo "migrating"

tests:
  - hello Ada --times 2: assert result.output == "hello Ada\nhello Ada\n"
  - hi Ada: assert result.output == "hello Ada\n"
  - resize cat.jpg -w 100: assert result.output == "cat.jpg 100\n"
  - resize: assert result.exit_code == 2
  - tag --loud a b: assert result.output == "A\nB\n"
  - db migrate: assert result.exit_code == 0

$ cli run click.yaml -- hello Ada --times 2
hello Ada
hello Ada
$ cli run click.yaml -- resize cat.jpg -w 100
cat.jpg 100
$ cli run click.yaml -- tag --loud a b
A
B
$ cli run click.yaml db migrate
migrating

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
• Commands, groups (db.migrate) and aliases (hello|hi)
  • Shorthand and explicit params with the same meaning as for Typer: a name with -- is an option, anything else is a positional argument, ! or required: true makes it required, and short, default and help are passed on
  • types, command config, global_params, callbacks, pre_run, post_run and command templates
  • Generic params, written as Click decorators
  • vars, imports, functions, includes, shell lines and cli test

docs.title: What differs from Typer
docs.text:
Feature With use_click: true Generic params A string param is a Click decorator such as "@click.option('--loud', is_flag=True)". A Typer signature entry is rejected. types A plain type (Count: int, Count: int = 1) works with both backends. A full definition is a Click decorator, Loud: "@click.option('--loud', is_flag=True)"; a typer.Option(...) definition is rejected with an error that names the command. Inline typer.Option(...) in a shorthand param Rejected. Use a Click decorator. List types --tag: list[str] can be given several times and arrives as a tuple, not a list. Boolean options --loud: bool = False is a --loud/--no-loud switch, also when it has a short form. config.rich_help_panel Passed to rich-click as panel. The generated code then requires rich-click. --version output <program>, version <version> instead of <name>, <version>.

A manifest that uses something the Click backend cannot express stops with an error such as:

~ error in tools.yaml: command `pack`: param `level` uses types.Level, which is a Typer definition (...)

docs.title: rich-click is optional
docs.text:
The generated module starts with:

try:
    import rich_click as click
except ImportError:  # plain help output when rich-click is not installed
    import click

With rich-click installed the help is formatted with Rich. Without it the same CLI runs on plain Click, which cliffy always installs. cli build reads this import and ships rich-click with the built CLI.

docs.title: Building
docs.text: cli build reads the import of rich_click from the generated code and bundles rich-click instead of Typer, so the manifest does not have to list it under requires.

docs.title: Typer notes
docs.text:
• Typer depends on Rich, so generated CLIs print styled help and tracebacks without extra setup.

  • Typer adds --install-completion and --show-completion to every CLI. Turn them off with:

    cli_options:
  add_completion: false

  • Anything from the Typer documentation that fits in a function signature or body can be used in types, generic params and run scripts.

docs.title: Building executables
docs.text:
cli build turns a manifest into one file that you can hand to someone else. The manifest stays the same; --target chooses what kind of file you get.

zipapp (default) script native What you get notes, a Python zipapp with the dependencies inside notes.py, readable Python with the dependencies declared at the top notes, a compiled executable with its own Python inside The other machine needs A compatible Python uv, or Python with the dependencies installed Nothing. Same operating system and CPU as the build machine Network on the other machine No The first run, to download the dependencies No The build machine needs Network or a pip cache for the dependencies Nothing Rust (cargo), uv and network Build time 2 s Under 1 s 1 min File size 1.8 MB 1 to 12 kB 30 MB First start 0.2 s 0.2 s with the dependencies in uv's cache 1.5 s Later starts 0.05 s 0.05 s 0.05 s Written to disk on the other machine 8 MB in ~/.shiv uv's cache 110 MB in the user's data and cache directories

The numbers were measured on an Apple Silicon Mac with Python 3.11 for a CLI whose only dependency is Typer. They show the proportions; yours will differ.

Whatever the target, the file holds the generated CLI and does not need cliffy. $ lines with pipes, redirects or && use a small helper from pybash; cli build copies it into the file, so pybash is not needed either.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
$ cli build notes.yaml -o dist
+ notes built 📦
  dist/notes (single file, needs Python >=3.10, 1.8 MB)
  run it with: ./dist/notes
$ ./dist/notes --version
notes, 0.1.0

Without -o, the file is written to the current directory. Several manifests can be built in one call, and a CLI that is already loaded can be built by name:

$ cli build notes.yaml hello.yaml -o dist
$ cli build notes -o dist --target script

When a build fails, the reason is printed and cli build exits with 1.

A file written in a blueprint's spec is built the same way for every target; the blueprint is applied at build time and is not shipped.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Every target ships the packages under requires:

requires:
  - tabulate>=0.9.0

Unlike cli load, building from a manifest does not need those packages to be installed in your environment.

The framework the generated code imports (Typer, or rich-click with use_click) is added for you, pinned to the version installed next to cliffy unless requires names it.

docs.title: zipapp
docs.text:
The default. A zipapp built with shiv contains the CLI and its dependencies, downloaded with pip at build time. The other machine needs Python and nothing else.

  • The line printed after a build says which Python the file needs. The file checks this when it starts and stops with a readable message on an unsupported interpreter.

  • The file starts with a #! line that selects the Python to run it, /usr/bin/env python3 by default. Change it with --python:

    $ cli build notes.yaml -o dist --python "/usr/bin/env python3.12"

  • Packages with compiled code are bundled for the platform and Python version you build on. Build on the same kind of system you will run on, or stick to pure-Python dependencies.

  • Building the same manifest twice in the same environment gives an identical file.
  • On first run, shiv unpacks the bundled packages to ~/.shiv. Set the SHIV_ROOT environment variable to use another directory.

docs.title: script
docs.text:
$ cli build notes.yaml -o dist --target script
+ notes built 📦
  dist/notes.py (single file, needs uv, or Python >=3.11 with typer==0.27.3 installed, 3.6 kB)
  run it with: ./dist/notes.py (or: uv run dist/notes.py)
  uv downloads the dependencies the first time the script runs

The result is the Python that cli render shows, with three things in front of it: a #! line, the dependencies as inline script metadata and a check of the Python version.

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# dependencies = [
#     "typer==0.27.3",
# ]
# ///
  • With uv installed, ./dist/notes.py and uv run dist/notes.py both work. uv creates an environment with exactly the listed dependencies, downloads them on the first run and reuses them afterwards.
  • Without uv, install the dependencies yourself and run python dist/notes.py.
  • Nothing is downloaded at build time, so the build works offline and gives the same file every time.
  • The file is plain text: it can be read, reviewed in a diff and edited. This is the target to pick when the reader should see what they run.
  • --python replaces the #! line, for example --python "/usr/bin/env python3" for machines without uv.

docs.title: native
docs.text:
$ cli build notes.yaml -o dist --target native
+ notes built 📦
  dist/notes (single file, needs nothing installed, runs on macOS arm64, 30.1 MB)
  run it with: ./dist/notes
  the first run unpacks its Python 3.11 (75.0 MB) into the user's data directory, without network access; later runs start right away

The result is one compiled executable. It contains a complete Python with the CLI and its dependencies already installed, so the other machine needs neither Python nor network access.

docs.title: What the build machine needs
docs.text:
• Rust. cargo compiles the launcher. Install it from rustup.rs.
  • uv. It downloads the standalone Python and installs the CLI into it. See Installing uv.
  • Network access, for that Python, the dependencies and the source of the launcher.
  • About a minute, and 700 MB of temporary disk space that is freed when the build ends.

When cargo or uv is missing, cli build says so and how to install it before it starts.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
1. uv downloads a standalone Python of the version cliffy runs on.
  2. The generated CLI is packaged as a wheel and installed into that Python together with its dependencies.
  3. The result is embedded in PyApp, a launcher written in Rust, which is compiled into the executable.

docs.title: What happens on the other machine
docs.text:
• The executable runs on the operating system and CPU architecture it was built on. Build on each platform you want to support. The target is available on macOS and Linux.
  • The first run unpacks the embedded Python, which takes a second or two, and then starts the CLI. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is installed with pip. Later runs only check that the directory exists.
  • The Python is unpacked to pyapp/<name> in the user's data directory (~/Library/Application Support on macOS, ~/.local/share on Linux), and a copy of the archive is kept in the cache directory (~/Library/Caches/pyapp, ~/.cache/pyapp). Together that is about 110 MB for a small CLI. Set PYAPP_INSTALL_DIR_<NAME>, with the name of the CLI in upper case, to unpack somewhere else. Delete the directory to reclaim the space; the next run unpacks it again.
  • Every argument goes to your CLI. PyApp's own self commands are turned off.

--python does not apply to this target.

docs.title: Things that hold for every target
docs.text:
• Values taken from env in vars are fixed at build time. See Vars and Jinja.
  • External commands that the CLI runs with $ lines are not bundled. They have to exist on the other machine.

docs.title: Check before you ship
docs.text:
$ cli test notes.yaml
$ cli build notes.yaml -o dist
$ ./dist/notes --help

docs.title: Commands, groups and aliases
docs.text:
Everything under commands becomes a command of your CLI. The key decides where the command lives and what it is called; the value decides what it does.

The snippets on this page come from one manifest, shown in full at the end.

docs.title: Three ways to write a command
docs.text:
# 1. A string: the whole value is the run script
  ping: print("pong")

  # 2. A list: each item is a line of the run script
  status:
    - print("checking...")
    - $ echo "all good"

  # 3. A mapping: the full form
  greet:
    help: Greet a customer
    params:
      - name: str = "friend"
    run: |
      print(f"Welcome, {name}!")

Use the short forms for one-liners and the mapping when you need help, params or anything else. The keys of the mapping are listed in the manifest reference.

$ cli run commands.yaml ping
pong
$ cli run commands.yaml greet
Welcome, friend!

Command names may contain letters, digits, - and _.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A dot in the key puts the command in a group. Groups are created as needed and can be nested.

  # A dot nests a command inside a group: `shop orders list`
  orders.create:
    help: Create an order
    params:
      - item: str!
    run: print(f"created order for {item}")

  orders.ship:
    help: Ship an order
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: print(f"shipped order {number}")

  # Groups nest as deep as you like: `shop stock warehouse count`
  stock.warehouse.count: print("42 items")

  # A command with help and no run script sets the help text of the group
  orders:
    help: Manage customer orders

$ cli run commands.yaml orders create book
created order for book
$ cli run commands.yaml stock warehouse count
42 items
$ cli run commands.yaml -- orders --help
...
╭─ Commands ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ create  Create an order                                                    │
│ ship    Ship an order                                                      │
│ list    List all orders                                                    │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

To describe a group, add an entry with the group's name that has help and no run, like orders above. A name is either a group or a command: if orders had a run script while orders.create exists, the group would take the name and the script could not be reached.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
# `shop customers add` and `shop customers new` run the same code
  customers.add|new:
    help: Add a customer
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: print(f"added {name}")

  # The aliases field does the same without touching the key
  version-info:
    help: Show build details
    aliases: [vi]
    run: print("build 7")
  • | in the key adds aliases to the last part of the name: customers.add|new gives customers add and customers new.
  • The aliases list does the same from inside the command.

Aliases are hidden from --help. When a manifest defines aliases in its keys, the CLI gets an --aliases option that lists them:

$ cli run commands.yaml -- --aliases

Command             Aliases
--------            --------
customers.add       new

docs.title: One command for every group
docs.text:
A key that starts with (*) is added to every group. Inside that command, {(*)} is replaced with the group's name, in help, run, pre_run, post_run and params.

  # (*) adds this command to every group; {(*)} is replaced by the group name
  (*).list:
    help: List all {(*)}
    params:
      - --limit|-l: int = 10
    run: print(f"listing {limit} {(*)}")

$ cli run commands.yaml orders list
listing 10 orders
$ cli run commands.yaml -- customers list -l 3
listing 3 customers

docs.title: Run scripts
docs.text:
run is Python. Write it as a block (run: |) or as a list of lines. Lines that start with $ are shell commands, described in Shell commands.

Two hooks wrap the script. pre_run runs before run and post_run after it, in the same function, so all three share variables.

  deploy:
    help: Deploy the shop
    pre_run: print("1. pre_run")
    run: print("2. run")
    post_run: print("3. post_run")

$ cli run commands.yaml deploy
1. pre_run
2. run
3. post_run

Hooks are most useful together with command templates, which let several commands share them.

To stop a command with an exit code, raise typer.Exit:

run: |
  if not ready:
      print("not ready")
      raise typer.Exit(code=1)

docs.title: Help text
docs.text:
help on a command is shown in the command list and at the top of the command's own --help. Because run is the body of a Python function, a docstring on its first line works as well:

  about:
    run: |
      """Show what this CLI is for"""
      print("A demo shop")

docs.title: Command settings
docs.text:
config passes extra settings to Typer for one command.

  migrate:
    help: Run the old migration tool
    run: print("migrating")
    config:
      deprecated: true
      hidden: true
      epilog: Use `shop deploy` instead.
Key Effect hidden Leave the command out of --help. deprecated Mark the command as deprecated and print a warning when it runs. epilog Text shown at the end of the command's help. short_help Text for the command list, when it should differ from help. no_args_is_help Show help when the command is called without arguments. context_settings Click context settings, for example help_option_names.

All keys are in the manifest reference.

docs.title: The complete example
docs.text:
commands.yaml
name: shop
version: 0.1.0
help: Groups, aliases and command options

cli_options:
  add_completion: false
  no_args_is_help: true

commands:
  # 1. A string: the whole value is the run script
  ping: print("pong")

  # 2. A list: each item is a line of the run script
  status:
    - print("checking...")
    - $ echo "all good"

  # 3. A mapping: the full form
  greet:
    help: Greet a customer
    params:
      - name: str = "friend"
    run: |
      print(f"Welcome, {name}!")

  # A dot nests a command inside a group: `shop orders list`
  orders.create:
    help: Create an order
    params:
      - item: str!
    run: print(f"created order for {item}")

  orders.ship:
    help: Ship an order
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: print(f"shipped order {number}")

  # Groups nest as deep as you like: `shop stock warehouse count`
  stock.warehouse.count: print("42 items")

  # A command with help and no run script sets the help text of the group
  orders:
    help: Manage customer orders

  # `shop customers add` and `shop customers new` run the same code
  customers.add|new:
    help: Add a customer
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: print(f"added {name}")

  # The aliases field does the same without touching the key
  version-info:
    help: Show build details
    aliases: [vi]
    run: print("build 7")

  # (*) adds this command to every group; {(*)} is replaced by the group name
  (*).list:
    help: List all {(*)}
    params:
      - --limit|-l: int = 10
    run: print(f"listing {limit} {(*)}")

  deploy:
    help: Deploy the shop
    pre_run: print("1. pre_run")
    run: print("2. run")
    post_run: print("3. post_run")

  migrate:
    help: Run the old migration tool
    run: print("migrating")
    config:
      deprecated: true
      hidden: true
      epilog: Use `shop deploy` instead.

  about:
    run: |
      """Show what this CLI is for"""
      print("A demo shop")

tests:
  - ping: assert result.output == "pong\n"
  - greet: assert result.output == "Welcome, friend!\n"
  - orders create book: assert result.output == "created order for book\n"
  - orders ship 7: assert result.output == "shipped order 7\n"
  - stock warehouse count: assert result.output == "42 items\n"
  - orders --help: assert "Manage customer orders" in result.output
  - customers new Ada: assert result.output == "added Ada\n"
  - vi: assert result.output == "build 7\n"
  - orders list: assert result.output == "listing 10 orders\n"
  - customers list -l 3: assert result.output == "listing 3 customers\n"
  - orders list --help: assert "List all orders" in result.output
  - deploy: assert result.output == "1. pre_run\n2. run\n3. post_run\n"
  - migrate: assert "migrating" in result.output
  - --help: assert "migrate" not in result.output
  - about --help: assert "Show what this CLI is for" in result.output
  - --aliases: assert "customers.add" in result.output

docs.title: Hot-reload dev loop
docs.text:
While you are writing a manifest, there are three ways to try your changes. They differ in how much they install.

Command Installs the CLI Use it for cli run notes.yaml -- <args> no A quick one-off call. cli load notes.yaml, then cli update notes yes Using the CLI by name; reload by hand. cli dev notes.yaml yes Reloading automatically on every save.

docs.title: cli dev
docs.text:
$ cli dev notes.yaml
🔄 Watching notes.yaml for changes...

Leave this running and edit the manifest. Each time you save, cliffy regenerates and reloads the CLI:

✨ Reloaded notes CLI v0.1.0 ✨

In a second terminal, with the same environment active, the notes command always reflects the last save. Stop the watcher with Ctrl+C.

The watcher follows every file the CLI is generated from: the manifest, the manifests it lists under includes and, for a file written in a blueprint's spec, the blueprint's Python file. Saving any of them reloads the CLI.

Note

Nothing is loaded until the first change. Save the file once, or run cli load notes.yaml before starting, to get the command right away.

docs.title: Run a command on every reload
docs.text:
--run-cli runs your CLI after each reload with the arguments that follow. It is a quick way to re-check one command while you work on it:

$ cli dev notes.yaml --run-cli tags list
🔄 Watching notes.yaml for changes...

✨ Reloaded notes CLI v0.1.0 ✨
general (1)
travel (1)

Put -- before the arguments when they include options:

$ cli dev notes.yaml --run-cli -- list --tag home
$ cli dev notes.yaml --run-cli -- --help

A mistake in the manifest prints an error in the watcher's terminal. Fix the file and save again; the watcher keeps running.

docs.title: Managing loaded CLIs
docs.text:
$ cli list            # what is loaded, from which manifest, and how long ago
$ cli info notes      # version, requirements and the stored manifest
$ cli update notes    # regenerate from the manifest path recorded at load time
$ cli remove notes    # uninstall
$ cli remove-all      # uninstall everything cliffy loaded

cli ls, cli reload, cli rm and cli rm-all are aliases for these. Details are in the CLI reference.

Loading writes a small launcher script named after the CLI into the bin directory of the environment. cliffy only replaces or deletes that file while it is exactly the launcher it wrote. If a file with the name of your CLI is already there (pip, say), cli load stops and asks you to rename the CLI. If you edited the launcher, cli remove removes nothing, tells you which file is in the way and leaves the CLI loaded and working; move or delete that file and remove the CLI again.

While cli dev runs, reloads happen one at a time and each one reads the manifest when it starts, so after a burst of saves the loaded CLI is the one of the last save.

Loaded CLIs belong to the Python environment cliffy is installed in. They are available whenever that environment is active and disappear with it.

docs.title: Editor setup
docs.text: cliffy publishes a JSON schema for manifests. An editor that understands it completes keys, shows their descriptions and marks mistakes while you type.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Install the YAML extension, then point a manifest at the schema with a comment on its first line.

Schema from GitHubLocal schema 
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jaykv/cliffy/refs/heads/main/examples/cliffy_schema.json
name: mycli
version: 0.1.0

This always uses the schema of the latest development version.

$ cli init mycli --raw --json-schema
+ mycli.yaml
+ cliffy_schema.json

This writes cliffy_schema.json, which matches your installed version, next to a new manifest that already has the comment:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=cliffy_schema.json

Other editors that use yaml-language-server, such as Neovim and Helix, read the same comment.

docs.title: Highlighting Python inside YAML
docs.text: Run scripts are Python inside YAML strings, which editors show as plain text. The YAML Embedded Languages extension for VS Code adds syntax highlighting to those blocks.

docs.title: Checking from the command line
docs.text:
$ cli validate mycli.yaml
Manifest mycli.yaml is valid

cli validate checks the same schema, plus the requires of the manifest and the code that is generated from it. See the CLI reference.

docs.title: Generating docs
docs.text: cli docs writes a reference page for your CLI from its manifest: the description, every command with its params and aliases, and the examples you provide.

docs.title: Add examples
docs.text:
examples is a list of command lines with a description each. They are part of the documentation cli docs writes, and the generated CLI shows them at the end of its own --help:

 Examples:

 $ notes add "buy milk" --tag home  # Add a note tagged home.

 $ notes ls --tag home  # Show only the notes tagged home.

Write an example as you would type it, starting with the name of the CLI. It is shown as written: quotes, brackets and backslashes are not interpreted. The help of a single command does not repeat the examples.

examples:
  - command: notes add "buy milk" --tag home
    description: Add a note tagged home.
  - command: notes ls --tag home
    description: Show only the notes tagged home.

Give every example a description. A plain string is accepted too, but is rendered with None in place of the description.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text:
$ cli docs notes.yaml
+ notes.md
Option Values Default --format, -f md, rst, html md --output-dir, -o an existing directory the current directory 
$ mkdir -p site
$ cli docs notes.yaml --format html --output-dir site
+ notes.html

docs.title: What the page contains
docs.text:
For the notes manifest from the Quickstart, the Markdown output starts like this:

# notes v0.1.0

Keep short notes in a JSON file

## Commands

### add
Add a note

Parameters:
- text: Text
- tag: Tag

### list|ls
List notes, optionally filtered by tag

Parameters:
- --tag: str (default: "")

Aliases: ls

and ends with the examples:

## Examples

```bash
notes add "buy milk" --tag home
```
Add a note tagged home.
  • Commands are listed in manifest order, under the key they have in the manifest.
  • Shorthand and explicit params are listed with their type; explicit params also show their help text. Generic params (plain strings) are left out.
  • Pass a manifest path or the name of a loaded CLI. A loaded CLI is documented from the manifest path recorded by cli load.

docs.title: Includes and merging
docs.text: includes merges other YAML files into a manifest. Use it to share functions, types and commands between several CLIs.

docs.title: An include file
docs.text:
An include file looks like a manifest without name and version:

shared/common.yaml
imports:
  - import json

vars:
  team: platform

functions:
  - |
    def as_json(data: dict) -> str:
        return json.dumps(data, sort_keys=True)

types:
  Service: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Name of the service")

commands:
  health:
    help: Report service health
    params:
      - service: Service
    run: |
      print(as_json({"service": service, "status": "ok"}))

  whoami:
    help: Show the owning team
    run: print(team)

tests:
  - health api: assert '"ok"' in result.output

It may contain commands, functions, imports, types, vars, requires, cli_options and tests. In an include file, functions must be a list.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
ops.yaml
name: ops
version: 0.1.0
help: Commands shared between CLIs through includes

includes:
  - shared/common.yaml

commands:
  restart:
    help: Restart a service
    params:
      - service: Service
    run: |
      print(as_json({"service": service, "action": "restart"}))

  # Same key as in the include: the keys set here win, the rest is inherited
  whoami:
    help: Show who owns this CLI

tests:
  - restart api: assert '"restart"' in result.output
  - whoami: assert result.output == "platform\n"
  - whoami --help: assert "Show who owns this CLI" in result.output

$ cli run ops.yaml health api
{"service": "api", "status": "ok"}
$ cli run ops.yaml restart api
{"action": "restart", "service": "api"}
$ cli run ops.yaml whoami
platform

restart is defined in ops.yaml and uses the Service type and the as_json function from the include. health comes entirely from the include.

Paths are relative to the manifest

shared/common.yaml is looked up next to the manifest that includes it first, and in the current working directory after that. A manifest that includes itself, directly or through another file, is reported as a circular include. cli dev watches included files too.

docs.title: How files are merged
docs.text:
All included files are merged together first. The result is then merged into your manifest.

Kind of value Rule Example Mapping Merged key by key, at every level. commands, types, vars, and the keys of a single command List Items from the include are added, without duplicates. requires, tests, functions and imports when both are lists Anything else The value in your manifest wins. a command's help or run

In the example, both files define whoami. The command keeps its run script from the include and takes help from ops.yaml.

Two details to keep in mind:

  • When the same key holds a list in one file and a block of text in the other, your manifest's value is kept and the include's is dropped. Write imports as a list in both files if both need imports.
  • Include files are merged in the order they are listed. When two of them set the same key to different values, the one listed first wins.

docs.title: Variables in include files
docs.text: Each file is rendered on its own. {{ team }} works inside shared/common.yaml, where team is defined, but not inside ops.yaml. The Python variable team is available to every command in the merged CLI, which is why whoami can print it. See Vars and Jinja.

docs.title: Manifest basics
docs.text: A manifest is one YAML file that describes one CLI. This page explains its parts and how cliffy turns them into Python. For a hands-on introduction, start with the Quickstart.

docs.title: The smallest manifest
docs.text:
Three keys are required: name, version and commands.

hello.yaml
name: hello
version: 0.1.0

commands:
  world: print("hello world")

$ cli run hello.yaml world
hello world

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
Key What it is for Guide name The command people type. version Printed by --version. Must be a string, so write "1.0" with quotes. help Description shown at the top of --help. commands The commands and the code they run. Commands, groups and aliases imports Python imports for the generated module. below functions Helper functions shared by all commands. below vars Variables you can reuse across the manifest. Vars and Jinja types Named parameter definitions. Params and types global_params Params added to commands. Templates and global params command_templates Reusable params, hooks and settings. Templates and global params includes Other manifests to merge in. Includes and merging requires Python packages the CLI depends on. below cli_options Options for the CLI application object. below use_click Generate Click code instead of Typer. Click and Typer backends tests Commands to run and assertions to check. Testing manifests examples Example command lines, shown in --help and in generated docs. Generating docs

Keys that cliffy does not know are ignored. The manifest reference lists every key with its type and default.

docs.title: How a manifest becomes Python
docs.text:
cliffy writes a single Python module from the manifest, in this order:

  1. import subprocess, import typer and the lines from imports
  2. one variable per entry in vars
  3. the Typer application, with --version built in
  4. the functions
  5. one function per command, registered with Typer

Each command's run script becomes the body of its function, and its params become the function's arguments. That is the whole model: anything you can write in a Python function, you can write in run.

To read the generated module for any manifest:

$ cli render hello.yaml

The output is the module itself, so cli render hello.yaml > hello.py writes a file you can run. The closing # Rendered ... line goes to the error stream and does not end up in that file.

docs.title: Imports and functions
docs.text:
imports: |
  import json
  from pathlib import Path

functions:
  - |
    def load(path: str) -> dict:
        return json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
  - |
    def branch() -> str:
        out = $ git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
        return out.decode().strip()

imports is a block of text or a list of lines. functions is a list with one function per item. subprocess and typer are always imported, so typer.Exit, typer.confirm and friends are available everywhere.

Write functions as a list when a function contains shell lines. A single block of text is also accepted, but $ lines inside it are not translated.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
List the packages your code imports under requires, using the same specifiers as pip:

requires:
  - tabulate>=0.9.0
  - rich
  • cli load, cli run, cli test and cli validate stop with missing requirement when a listed package is not installed in the environment cliffy runs in.
  • cli build downloads the listed packages and bundles them into the executable.

docs.title: CLI options
docs.text:
cli_options is passed to the Typer application as keyword arguments. Two common settings:

cli_options:
  add_completion: false   # hide --install-completion and --show-completion
  no_args_is_help: true   # print help when the CLI is called without a command

docs.title: Check, run, load
docs.text:
Command What it does cli validate hello.yaml Checks the YAML, the schema, the requires and that the generated code imports. cli render hello.yaml Prints the generated Python. cli run hello.yaml -- <args> Runs the CLI once without installing it. cli test hello.yaml Runs the tests section. cli load hello.yaml Installs the CLI as a command in the current environment.

All of them are described in the CLI reference.

docs.title: YAML pitfalls
docs.text:
Manifests mix YAML, Jinja and Python, and each has its own special characters.

A colon followed by a space ends a YAML key. This one-line command breaks, because of : inside the string:

commands:
  status: print("status: ok")      # YAML error

Use a block instead:

commands:
  status: |
    print("status: ok")

Quote values that YAML would not read as text. version: 1.0 is a number and is rejected; version: "1.0" works. The same applies to values in vars.

Quote a one-line command that starts with >. YAML treats a leading > as its own syntax, so write run: "> ls *.txt".

Double braces belong to Jinja. {{ name }} is replaced when the manifest is loaded. To get literal double braces into your Python, see Vars and Jinja.

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text: cliffy publishes a JSON schema for manifests, which gives you completion and validation while you type. See Editor setup.

docs.title: Params and types
docs.text:
Params are the arguments and options of a command. Inside run they are ordinary Python variables. A params list accepts three forms, and you can mix them in one command.

Form Looks like Use it when Shorthand - name: str! You want the shortest syntax. Explicit - name: image and more keys You want help text. Generic - 'path: str = typer.Argument(...)' You need the full Typer API for one param.

To reuse one definition across commands, give it a name under types.

docs.title: Shorthand
docs.text:
Each entry is name: type.

  copy:
    help: Shorthand params
    params:
      - source: str!              # required argument
      - target: str = "out.txt"   # optional argument with a default
      - label: str                # optional argument, None when omitted
      - --count|-c: int = 1       # option with a short alias and a default
      - --force|-f: bool = False  # boolean flag
      - --owner: str!             # required option
      - --dry-run: bool = False   # hyphens become underscores in Python
    run: |
      print(source, target, label, count, force, owner, dry_run)
You write You get source: str! A required positional argument. target: str = "out.txt" An optional argument with a default. label: str An optional argument that is None when omitted. --count|-c: int = 1 The option --count with the short form -c. --force|-f: bool = False A flag. force is True when --force or -f is passed. --owner: str! A required option. --dry-run: bool = False An option whose variable is dry_run.

Rules:

  • A name that starts with -- is an option. Anything else is a positional argument.
  • ! after the type makes the param required.
  • The text after = is a Python expression, so string defaults need quotes: str = "out.txt".
  • Hyphens in a name become underscores in the variable.
  • Positional arguments are read from the command line in the order you list them, so put required ones first.
$ cli run params.yaml -- copy a.txt --owner me
a.txt out.txt None 1 False me False
$ cli run params.yaml -- copy a.txt b.txt c -c 3 -f --owner me --dry-run
a.txt b.txt c 3 True me True

Boolean options without a short form

--dry-run: bool = False is generated without explicit option names, so Typer also adds the negative form --no-dry-run. Options declared with a short form, such as --force|-f, get only the names you wrote.

docs.title: Explicit
docs.text:
Each entry is a mapping. This is the only form with a help key.

  resize:
    help: Explicit params
    params:
      - name: image
        type: str
        required: true
        help: Image to resize
      - name: --width
        type: int
        default: 800
        short: -w
        help: Target width in pixels
      - name: --format
        type: str
        default: png
        help: Output format
    run: |
      print(image, width, format)
Key Meaning name Param name. Start it with -- to make an option; without it the param is a positional argument. type A Python type such as str, int, float, bool, or a name from types. default Default value. String defaults are quoted for you when type is str. help Text shown in --help. short Short option name including the dash, such as -w. Options only. required true to make the param required. 
$ cli run params.yaml -- resize cat.jpg -w 100 --format gif
cat.jpg 100 gif

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
types gives a name to a type or to a complete Typer parameter definition. Use the name wherever a type is expected, in shorthand or explicit params.

types:
  Level: int = typer.Option(1, "--level", "-l", min=1, max=5, help="Compression level")
  Source: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to read")

  pack:
    help: Params that reuse the types section
    params:
      - source: Source
      - level: Level
    run: |
      print(source, level)

A complete definition is everything that follows the param name in a Python signature: the type, then typer.Argument(...) or typer.Option(...). This gives you help text, validation (min, max), prompts (prompt=True), environment variables (envvar="NAME") and the rest of the Typer parameter API. It replaces everything the param entry says except its name, so a default or help written next to it is not used.

A plain type is an alias:

types:
  Count: int = 1

commands:
  repeat:
    params:
      - --times: Count       # the option --times, an int, default 1
      - --retries: Count = 3 # a default on the param wins
    run: print(times, retries)

The param keeps what its own entry says: --times is an option because of its name, and an explicit param keeps its help. Plain types work with both backends.

$ cli run params.yaml -- pack data.csv
data.csv 1
$ cli run params.yaml -- pack data.csv -l 9
╭─ Error ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Invalid value for '--level' / '-l': 9 is not in the range 1<=x<=5.         │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

docs.title: Generic
docs.text:
A plain string is copied into the function signature exactly as written. Quote the whole entry so that YAML reads it as a string.

  tail:
    help: Raw Typer signatures
    params:
      - 'path: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to follow")'
      - 'lines: int = typer.Option(10, "--lines", "-n", min=1, help="Lines to show")'
    run: |
      print(path, lines)

A Typer definition also works in a shorthand entry

- name: str = typer.Option("World", "--name") is passed through as written. Use types when several commands share the definition.

docs.title: Where else params appear
docs.text:
• global_params and command_templates.<name>.params accept the same three forms. See Command templates and global params.
  • With use_click: true, params are translated to Click decorators. Shorthand and explicit params mean the same; generic params and full definitions in types are written as Click decorators. See Click and Typer backends.

docs.title: The complete example
docs.text:
params.yaml
name: params
version: 0.1.0
help: One command per way of declaring parameters

types:
  Level: int = typer.Option(1, "--level", "-l", min=1, max=5, help="Compression level")
  Source: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to read")

commands:
  copy:
    help: Shorthand params
    params:
      - source: str!              # required argument
      - target: str = "out.txt"   # optional argument with a default
      - label: str                # optional argument, None when omitted
      - --count|-c: int = 1       # option with a short alias and a default
      - --force|-f: bool = False  # boolean flag
      - --owner: str!             # required option
      - --dry-run: bool = False   # hyphens become underscores in Python
    run: |
      print(source, target, label, count, force, owner, dry_run)

  resize:
    help: Explicit params
    params:
      - name: image
        type: str
        required: true
        help: Image to resize
      - name: --width
        type: int
        default: 800
        short: -w
        help: Target width in pixels
      - name: --format
        type: str
        default: png
        help: Output format
    run: |
      print(image, width, format)

  pack:
    help: Params that reuse the types section
    params:
      - source: Source
      - level: Level
    run: |
      print(source, level)

  tail:
    help: Raw Typer signatures
    params:
      - 'path: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to follow")'
      - 'lines: int = typer.Option(10, "--lines", "-n", min=1, help="Lines to show")'
    run: |
      print(path, lines)

tests:
  - copy a.txt --owner me: assert result.output == "a.txt out.txt None 1 False me False\n"
  - copy a.txt b.txt c -c 3 -f --owner me --dry-run: assert result.output == "a.txt b.txt c 3 True me True\n"
  - copy a.txt: assert result.exit_code == 2
  - resize cat.jpg: assert result.output == "cat.jpg 800 png\n"
  - resize cat.jpg -w 100 --format gif: assert result.output == "cat.jpg 100 gif\n"
  - pack data.csv: assert result.output == "data.csv 1\n"
  - pack data.csv -l 9: assert result.exit_code == 2
  - tail app.log: assert result.output == "app.log 10\n"
  - tail app.log -n 2: assert result.output == "app.log 2\n"

docs.title: Shell commands
docs.text: In any script, a line that starts with $ is run as an external command. cliffy uses pybash to translate these lines into subprocess calls, so you can move between Python and shell freely.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
hello: $ echo "hello from the shell"

  mixed:
    help: Mix Python and shell lines
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      print("python first")
      $ echo "then shell"
      if name == "ada":
          $ echo "shell lines can be indented"

$ echo "then shell" becomes subprocess.run(["echo", "then shell"]). The command is split into arguments the way a shell would split it, and is then started directly, without a shell in between. Shell lines follow Python indentation, so they can sit inside if blocks and loops.

$ lines work in run, pre_run, post_run, in callbacks, in functions written as a list, and as steps in tests. Run cli render to see the translation.

docs.title: Using Python values
docs.text:
f{expression} inserts the value of a Python expression into the command. The value is passed as a single argument, whatever it contains: spaces, quotes and ; are just text.

  say:
    help: Pass a Python value to a shell command
    params:
      - message: str!
    run: $ echo f{message} f{len(message)}

$ cli run shell.yaml say "two words"
two words 9

Everything an f-string accepts after the expression works too, and f{ } can be used inside quotes:

  price:
    help: f{ } takes f-string format specs, also inside quotes
    params:
      - amount: float!
    run: |
      out = $ echo "total: f{amount:,.2f}"
      print(out.decode().strip())

docs.title: Double braces are Jinja's
docs.text:
pybash also has a {{ expression }} form, which inserts str(expression). In a manifest, cliffy renders Jinja first, so {{ name }} is replaced with a var when the manifest is loaded and never reaches pybash. That is what you want for vars:

vars:
  data_file: tasks.json
commands:
  backup: $ cp {{ data_file }} {{ data_file }}.backup

For a value that only exists when the command runs, such as a param, use f{ }. If you prefer the double-brace form, put the lines in a Jinja raw block so they are left alone:

  whoami:
    help: Double braces belong to Jinja unless they are inside a raw block
    params:
      - user: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      out = $ echo {{ user.title() }}
      {% endraw %}
      print(out.decode().strip())

To write the markers themselves as text, escape them: \f{ and, inside a raw block, \{{.

docs.title: Capturing output
docs.text:
Assign a shell line to a variable, or wrap it in parentheses, to get its output as bytes. $(command) does the same in the middle of an expression:

  upper:
    help: Capture shell output in Python
    run: |
      out = $ echo captured
      print(out.decode().strip().upper())

  inline:
    help: Capture inline with parentheses
    run: print(($ echo inline).decode().strip())

  words:
    help: Capture in the middle of an expression with $( )
    run: print(len($(echo one two three).split()), "words")

$ cli run shell.yaml upper
CAPTURED
$ cli run shell.yaml words
3 words

A capture that is not wrapped in brackets runs to the end of the line.

docs.title: Pipes and redirection
docs.text:
Pipes and redirects are carried out by the generated CLI itself, without a shell:

  sorted:
    help: Pipes work without a shell
    run: $ printf 'b\na\n' | sort

  save:
    help: So does redirection
    run: |
      $ echo "saved" > shell-demo.txt
      $ cat shell-demo.txt

  errors-to-file:
    help: Redirect stderr on its own, together with stdout, or into a pipe
    run: |
      $ ls no-such-file 2> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file &> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file > shell-demo.txt 2>&1
