      lines = $ ls no-such-file |& wc -l
      print(int(lines), "line of errors")
Operator Meaning a | b Pipe the output of a into b a |& b Pipe output and errors < file Read input from a file > file, >> file Write or append output 2> file, 2>> file Write or append errors &> file, &>> file Write or append both 2>&1, >&2 Send errors to the output, or the output to the errors

docs.title: Chaining commands
docs.text:
&& runs the next command when the previous one succeeded, || when it failed, and ; in either case:

  chain:
    help: "&&, || and ; decide what runs next, like in a shell"
    run: |
      out = $ true && echo "first worked" || echo "first failed"
      print(out.decode().strip())
      out = $ false || echo "fallback" ; echo "always"
      print(out.decode().split())

Capturing a chain captures the output of every command that ran.

docs.title: Long commands and comments
docs.text:
A $ or > line that ends with a backslash continues on the next line. An unquoted # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line:

  longest:
    help: "A trailing backslash continues a command, a # starts a comment"
    run: |
      $ printf '%s\n' pear fig banana \
          | sort \
          | tail -n 1 > shell-demo.txt  # the last one in alphabetical order
      $ echo "a # inside quotes is text" >> shell-demo.txt
      print(open("shell-demo.txt").read())

A captured command (out = $ ...) has to fit on one line.

docs.title: When you need a real shell
docs.text:
$ lines never expand glob patterns (*.txt), ~ or environment variables ($HOME), and they do not support background jobs (&) or here-documents (<<). For those, start the line with > instead of $. The line is handed to the shell as written:

  texts:
    help: Glob patterns need a real shell
    run: "> ls *.txt"

This becomes subprocess.run("ls *.txt", shell=True). A one-line command that starts with > must be quoted, because > also has a meaning in YAML.

Values inserted with f{ } are quoted for the place they appear in, so a value is always one word of data and never shell syntax. Here name can be ; rm -rf ~ and nothing is removed:

  find:
    help: A value in a > line is quoted for the shell
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      > ls | grep -c f{name} || echo "nothing is called" f{name}

  glob:
    help: Splice a value in as shell syntax, here a glob pattern
    params:
      - pattern: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      > ls {{! pattern }}
      {% endraw %}

{{! expression }} is the exception: it splices the value in unquoted, so that it can be a glob pattern or several arguments. Like every double-brace form it has to sit in a raw block.

Never pass user input to {{! }}

A spliced value is interpreted by the shell. A parameter value such as ; rm -rf ~ would be executed. Use f{ } for anything that comes from a user, and prefer $ lines, which have no shell to inject into. See the Python documentation on subprocess security.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A shell line that fails does not stop the script. Check the result yourself when it matters:

  careless:
    help: A failing command does not stop the script
    run: |
      $ false
      print("still running")

  careful:
    help: Check the exit status yourself
    run: |
      result = subprocess.run(["false"])
      if result.returncode != 0:
          print("command failed")
          raise typer.Exit(code=result.returncode)

Two exceptions:

  • A command that does not exist raises FileNotFoundError.
  • A captured command (out = $ ...) raises subprocess.CalledProcessError when it exits with a non-zero status.

A shell line that cannot be translated is reported when the manifest is loaded, with the command it is in, the line and the column:

$ cli load deploy.yaml
~ error in deploy.yaml: command `ship`, run, line 2, column 11: running in the background with & is not supported in a $ command; use a > shell command
    $ sleep 5 &
              ^ 💔

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Output of $ lines goes straight to the terminal. It is not part of result.output in manifest tests; capture it and print it if you want to assert on it.
  • A CLI that only uses plain commands imports nothing but subprocess. Pipes, redirects, chains and values in > lines go through a small helper, pybash.runtime, which the generated code imports as _pybash. cli build copies that helper into the file it builds, so a built CLI does not need pybash.
  • Quoting follows POSIX shell rules: single quotes are literal, double quotes allow \" and \\, and a backslash escapes the next character. Quote or escape an operator to pass it as text: $ echo 'a && b' \| c.

docs.title: The complete example
docs.text:
shell.yaml
name: sh
version: 0.1.0
help: Shell commands in run scripts

functions:
  - |
    def current_branch() -> str:
        out = $ git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
        return out.decode().strip()

commands:
  hello: $ echo "hello from the shell"

  mixed:
    help: Mix Python and shell lines
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      print("python first")
      $ echo "then shell"
      if name == "ada":
          $ echo "shell lines can be indented"

  say:
    help: Pass a Python value to a shell command
    params:
      - message: str!
    run: $ echo f{message} f{len(message)}

  price:
    help: f{ } takes f-string format specs, also inside quotes
    params:
      - amount: float!
    run: |
      out = $ echo "total: f{amount:,.2f}"
      print(out.decode().strip())

  whoami:
    help: Double braces belong to Jinja unless they are inside a raw block
    params:
      - user: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      out = $ echo {{ user.title() }}
      {% endraw %}
      print(out.decode().strip())

  upper:
    help: Capture shell output in Python
    run: |
      out = $ echo captured
      print(out.decode().strip().upper())

  inline:
    help: Capture inline with parentheses
    run: print(($ echo inline).decode().strip())

  words:
    help: Capture in the middle of an expression with $( )
    run: print(len($(echo one two three).split()), "words")

  sorted:
    help: Pipes work without a shell
    run: $ printf 'b\na\n' | sort

  save:
    help: So does redirection
    run: |
      $ echo "saved" > shell-demo.txt
      $ cat shell-demo.txt

  errors-to-file:
    help: Redirect stderr on its own, together with stdout, or into a pipe
    run: |
      $ ls no-such-file 2> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file &> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file > shell-demo.txt 2>&1
      lines = $ ls no-such-file |& wc -l
      print(int(lines), "line of errors")

  chain:
    help: "&&, || and ; decide what runs next, like in a shell"
    run: |
      out = $ true && echo "first worked" || echo "first failed"
      print(out.decode().strip())
      out = $ false || echo "fallback" ; echo "always"
      print(out.decode().split())

  longest:
    help: "A trailing backslash continues a command, a # starts a comment"
    run: |
      $ printf '%s\n' pear fig banana \
          | sort \
          | tail -n 1 > shell-demo.txt  # the last one in alphabetical order
      $ echo "a # inside quotes is text" >> shell-demo.txt
      print(open("shell-demo.txt").read())

  texts:
    help: Glob patterns need a real shell
    run: "> ls *.txt"

  find:
    help: A value in a > line is quoted for the shell
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      > ls | grep -c f{name} || echo "nothing is called" f{name}

  glob:
    help: Splice a value in as shell syntax, here a glob pattern
    params:
      - pattern: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      > ls {{! pattern }}
      {% endraw %}

  careless:
    help: A failing command does not stop the script
    run: |
      $ false
      print("still running")

  careful:
    help: Check the exit status yourself
    run: |
      result = subprocess.run(["false"])
      if result.returncode != 0:
          print("command failed")
          raise typer.Exit(code=result.returncode)

tests:
  - hello: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - mixed ada: assert "python first" in result.output
  - say hi: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - upper: assert result.output == "CAPTURED\n"
  - inline: assert result.output == "inline\n"
  - words: assert result.output == "3 words\n"
  - price 1234.5: 'assert result.output == "total: 1,234.50\n"'
  - whoami ada: assert result.output == "Ada\n"
  - sorted: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - save: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - errors-to-file: assert result.output == "1 line of errors\n"
  - chain: assert result.output == "first worked\n['fallback', 'always']\n"
  - longest: assert result.output.splitlines()[0] == "pear" and "inside quotes" in result.output
  - find "; echo injected": assert result.exit_code == 0
  - glob "*.yaml": assert result.exit_code == 0
  - texts: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - careless: assert result.output == "still running\n"
  - careful: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - $ rm -f shell-demo.txt

docs.title: Command templates and global params
docs.text: Two features keep a manifest free of repetition. Global params add the same params to your commands. Command templates bundle params, hooks and settings under a name that commands opt into.

docs.title: Global params
docs.text:
global_params is a list of params, in any of the three forms.

types:
  Verbose: bool = typer.Option(False, "--verbose", "-v", help="Print extra detail")

global_params:
  - verbose: Verbose

The param is passed to the command itself, so it goes after the command name (files delete notes.txt --verbose) and is available in run as a normal variable.

Global params are added to every command, whether or not it has params of its own.

docs.title: Command templates
docs.text:
A template can hold params, pre_run, post_run and config.

command_templates:
  destructive:
    params:
      - --yes|-y: bool = False
    pre_run: |
      if not yes:
          typer.confirm("Are you sure?", abort=True)
    post_run: print("done")
    config:
      epilog: This command changes files on disk.

A command uses it with template: <name>:

commands:
  delete|rm:
    help: Delete a file
    template: destructive
    params:
      - path: str!
    pre_run: |
      if verbose:
          print(f"about to delete {path}")
    run: print(f"deleted {path}")
    post_run: print("cleaning up")

  wipe:
    help: Delete everything
    template: destructive
    run: print("wiped")
    config:
      epilog: There is no undo.

$ cli run templates.yaml -- delete notes.txt --yes --verbose
about to delete notes.txt
deleted notes.txt
cleaning up
done
$ cli run templates.yaml delete notes.txt
Are you sure? [y/N]: n
Aborted.

docs.title: How a template is merged into a command
docs.text:
Part Result params Template params first, then the command's own. pre_run Template pre_run, then the command's. post_run The command's post_run, then the template's. config Combined. A key set on the command overrides the same key from the template.

Together with global params, a command's arguments are ordered: global params, template params, command params.

The scripts therefore always run in this order:

  1. template pre_run
  2. command pre_run
  3. command run
  4. command post_run
  5. template post_run

All five are placed in one function, so a variable set in pre_run can be used in run.

In the example, wipe sets its own epilog, which replaces the one from the template, while delete keeps the template's:

$ cli run templates.yaml -- delete --help
...
╭─ Options ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --verbose  -v        Print extra detail                                    │
│ --yes      -y                                                              │
│ --help     -h        Show this message and exit.                           │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 This command changes files on disk.

A command can use one template. Naming a template that does not exist is an error when the manifest is loaded.

docs.title: The complete example
docs.text:
templates.yaml
name: files
version: 0.1.0
help: Command templates and global params

types:
  Verbose: bool = typer.Option(False, "--verbose", "-v", help="Print extra detail")

global_params:
  - verbose: Verbose

command_templates:
  destructive:
    params:
      - --yes|-y: bool = False
    pre_run: |
      if not yes:
          typer.confirm("Are you sure?", abort=True)
    post_run: print("done")
    config:
      epilog: This command changes files on disk.

commands:
  delete|rm:
    help: Delete a file
    template: destructive
    params:
      - path: str!
    pre_run: |
      if verbose:
          print(f"about to delete {path}")
    run: print(f"deleted {path}")
    post_run: print("cleaning up")

  wipe:
    help: Delete everything
    template: destructive
    run: print("wiped")
    config:
      epilog: There is no undo.

tests:
  - delete notes.txt --yes: assert result.output == "deleted notes.txt\ncleaning up\ndone\n"
  - rm notes.txt -y -v: assert result.output == "about to delete notes.txt\ndeleted notes.txt\ncleaning up\ndone\n"
  - wipe -y: assert result.output == "wiped\ndone\n"
  - wipe: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - delete --help: assert "This command changes files on disk." in result.output
  - wipe --help: assert "There is no undo." in result.output
  - wipe --help: assert "--verbose" in result.output

docs.title: Testing manifests
docs.text: A manifest can carry its own tests. Each test runs a command of your CLI and checks the result with Python assertions. cli test runs them without loading or building anything.

docs.title: Writing tests
docs.text:
tests:
  # A string starting with $ or > is a shell step, handy for setup and cleanup
  - $ rm -f counter.txt

  # A mapping is a test case: the command line, then the assertion to run
  - show: assert result.output == "0\n"
  - bump: assert result.exit_code == 0

  # Use a block when you need several statements
  - bump --by 2: |
      assert result.exit_code == 0
      assert result_text == "3"

  # Usage errors exit with code 2
  - bump --by nope: assert result.exit_code == 2

  # An uncaught exception is stored on the result
  - crash: |
      assert result.exit_code == 1
      assert isinstance(result.exception, ValueError)

  - "> rm -f counter.*"

$ cli test testing.yaml
✨ Invoking tests ✨

🪄 > counter show

⚗️ >
0


✅ 1 of 5

...

💚 All tests passed!

docs.title: Test cases
docs.text:
A test case is a one-key mapping:

- <command line>: <assertion code>

The command line is everything you would type after the CLI's name. It is split like a shell would split it, so quotes work: add "buy milk" --tag home.

The assertion code is Python. Two variables are available:

Variable What it is result The outcome of the command. Use result.output (everything the command printed), result.exit_code and result.exception. result_text result.output with leading and trailing whitespace removed.

Use assert statements. A test passes when the code runs without raising.

docs.title: Shell steps
docs.text:
An entry that is a plain string is a setup or cleanup step, not a test case. It must start with $ or > and follows the rules of shell commands: $ runs the command directly, > runs it through a shell (needed for glob patterns such as counter.*). Quote an entry that starts with >.

Entries run from top to bottom, so order the steps and cases accordingly.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
$ cli test testing.yaml
$ cli test testing.yaml --exitfirst

--exitfirst (or -x) stops at the first failing test.

A failing assertion is reported with its line:

💔 AssertionError: (line 1) > assert result.output == "1\n"

So is an assertion that raises something else, or that is not valid Python:

💔 NameError: name 'reslt' is not defined (line 1) > assert reslt.exit_code == 0

When the command itself raises, the exception is reported against the manifest: the command, the exception, and the line of the run, pre_run or post_run block it was raised on.

💥 command `add` raised KeyError: 'notes'
    run, line 2: data["notes"].append(text)

No Python traceback is printed. The assertions still run, so a test can expect the exception with assert isinstance(result.exception, KeyError). To see the full traceback of the command as well:

$ cli test testing.yaml --traceback

The run ends with one of three messages:

Last line Meaning Exit code 💚 All tests passed! Every test case passed. 0 💛 Some tests failed :( At least one passed and at least one failed. 1 All tests failed 💔 No test case passed. 1

The exit code is 0 only when every test case passed, so a CI job can run cli test mycli.yaml as a step of its own.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Colors and styles are removed from the output before your assertions run, so a test gives the same result in a terminal and on a CI system.
  • Tests run in the current directory and are not isolated from each other. A command that writes a file really writes it. Clean up with shell steps, as the example does.
  • Output of $ lines is not captured. It goes to the terminal and is not in result.output. Assert on the exit code, or capture the output in Python and print it. See Shell commands.

  • Keep : out of one-line assertions. YAML reads a colon followed by a space as the end of a key, so - show: assert result.output == "count: 0\n" is a YAML error. Use a block:

    - show: |
    assert result.output == "count: 0\n"

  • The counter counts test cases. ✅ 2 of 5 is the second test case of five. Shell steps are run but not counted, and a failed case keeps its number.

  • Shell steps are not checked. A step that exits with an error does not fail the run. Assert on the state it should have produced in the next test case. A step whose program cannot be started at all (it does not exist) ends the run with an error.

docs.title: The complete example
docs.text:
testing.yaml
name: counter
version: 0.1.0
help: A counter stored in a file, with tests

imports: |
  from pathlib import Path

functions:
  - |
    def read_count() -> int:
        path = Path("counter.txt")
        return int(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else 0

commands:
  show:
    help: Print the counter
    run: print(read_count())

  bump:
    help: Increase the counter
    params:
      - --by: int = 1
    run: |
      total = read_count() + by
      Path("counter.txt").write_text(str(total))
      print(total)

  crash:
    help: Always fails
    run: raise ValueError("boom")

tests:
  # A string starting with $ or > is a shell step, handy for setup and cleanup
  - $ rm -f counter.txt

  # A mapping is a test case: the command line, then the assertion to run
  - show: assert result.output == "0\n"
  - bump: assert result.exit_code == 0

  # Use a block when you need several statements
  - bump --by 2: |
      assert result.exit_code == 0
      assert result_text == "3"

  # Usage errors exit with code 2
  - bump --by nope: assert result.exit_code == 2

  # An uncaught exception is stored on the result
  - crash: |
      assert result.exit_code == 1
      assert isinstance(result.exception, ValueError)

  - "> rm -f counter.*"

docs.title: Vars and Jinja
docs.text: A manifest is rendered as a Jinja2 template before it is read as YAML. vars supplies the values. Use them for anything you would otherwise repeat: file names, URLs, defaults.

docs.title: Defining vars
docs.text:
vars:
  app: shop
  # Jinja expression, evaluated when the manifest is loaded
  region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"
  # A var can build on other vars
  image: "registry.example.com/{{ app }}:{{ region }}"
  # Numbers and booleans keep their type
  retries: 3
  # A value in braces is a Python expression instead of a string
  workdir: {os.getcwd()}

There are three kinds of value:

You write The var is app: shop The string shop. region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}" A string computed by a Jinja expression. image: "registry.example.com/{{ app }}:{{ region }}" A string built from other vars. retries: 3 The integer 3. Numbers and booleans keep their type. workdir: {os.getcwd()} The Python expression os.getcwd(), evaluated each time the CLI starts.

Quote a string value that starts with {{, and quote a number that should stay text (zip_code: "02134"). Braces around a value turn it into a Python expression.

A var name becomes a Python variable, so it has to be a valid identifier: data_file, not data-file. Names the generated code uses itself, such as cli and typer, are rejected too.

Vars can use each other in any order. cliffy resolves them before the rest of the file, and reports vars that refer to each other in a circle:

~ error loading manifest: vars.yaml: vars reference each other in a circle: a -> b -> a. A var cannot be built from itself.

docs.title: Using vars
docs.text:
Every var is available in two ways.

  show:
    help: Print the resolved variables
    run: |
      print("app={{ app }} region={{ region }} image={{ image }}")
      print(f"app={app} retries={retries + 1} cwd={workdir == os.getcwd()}")

$ cli run vars.yaml show
app=shop region=eu-west-1 image=registry.example.com/shop:eu-west-1
app=shop retries=4 cwd=True
  1. As a placeholder. {{ app }} is replaced with the value when the manifest is loaded. This works anywhere in the file: in scripts, help text, params, even in command names.
  2. As a Python variable. The generated module defines app = 'shop', so run scripts and functions can use app directly, and retries = 3 as a number. A var written with braces, like workdir, is only useful this way.

A placeholder for a name that is not defined is replaced with nothing, without an error. If output is unexpectedly empty, check the spelling with cli render.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
env holds the environment of the process that loads the manifest.

vars:
  region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"

$ DEPLOY_REGION=us-east-2 cli run vars.yaml show
app=shop region=us-east-2 image=registry.example.com/shop:us-east-2
app=shop retries=4 cwd=True

env can be used in vars and anywhere else in the file.

The value is read when the manifest is loaded or built and then fixed in the generated code. A CLI installed with cli load keeps the value it saw at load time. To read the environment each time a command runs, use Python instead:

imports:
  - import os

commands:
  region: print(os.environ.get("DEPLOY_REGION", "eu-west-1"))

docs.title: Loops and conditions
docs.text:
Jinja statements such as {% for %} and {% if %} work as long as the file is still valid YAML before rendering. Put them in YAML comments:

  # {% for stage in ['staging', 'production'] %}
  deploy.{{ stage }}:
    help: Deploy {{ app }} to {{ stage }}
    run: print("deploying {{ app }} to {{ stage }} in {{ region }}")
  # {% endfor %}

$ cli run vars.yaml deploy staging
deploying shop to staging in eu-west-1
$ cli run vars.yaml deploy production
deploying shop to production in eu-west-1

The loop produces one deploy.<stage> command per item.

docs.title: Literal braces
docs.text:
To keep double braces in your Python code, wrap them in {% raw %}:

  braces:
    help: Print literal double braces
    run: print({% raw %}"{{ not a variable }}"{% endraw %})

Single braces, as used in f-strings (f"{name}"), need no escaping.

docs.title: Comments are part of the template
docs.text:
The whole file is rendered, YAML comments included. That is what makes the loop above possible, and it means that double braces in a comment are read as a placeholder too. A comment such as # use {{ }} for placeholders is a Jinja syntax error, which is reported with its line:

~ error loading manifest: vars.yaml, line 12: Jinja syntax error: Expected an expression, got 'end of print statement'
    # use {{ }} for placeholders
  The whole file is a Jinja template, comments included. To keep braces as text, wrap them in {% raw %} and {% endraw %}.

Write the comment without double braces, or wrap them in {% raw %}.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: • Vars defined in an include file can be used as placeholders only inside that file.

docs.title: The complete example
docs.text:
vars.yaml
name: deployer
version: 0.1.0
help: Variables and Jinja templating

imports:
  - import os

vars:
  app: shop
  # Jinja expression, evaluated when the manifest is loaded
  region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"
  # A var can build on other vars
  image: "registry.example.com/{{ app }}:{{ region }}"
  # Numbers and booleans keep their type
  retries: 3
  # A value in braces is a Python expression instead of a string
  workdir: {os.getcwd()}

commands:
  show:
    help: Print the resolved variables
    run: |
      print("app={{ app }} region={{ region }} image={{ image }}")
      print(f"app={app} retries={retries + 1} cwd={workdir == os.getcwd()}")

  # {% for stage in ['staging', 'production'] %}
  deploy.{{ stage }}:
    help: Deploy {{ app }} to {{ stage }}
    run: print("deploying {{ app }} to {{ stage }} in {{ region }}")
  # {% endfor %}

  braces:
    help: Print literal double braces
    run: print({% raw %}"{{ not a variable }}"{% endraw %})

tests:
  - show: |
      assert result.output.splitlines() == [
          "app=shop region=eu-west-1 image=registry.example.com/shop:eu-west-1",
          "app=shop retries=4 cwd=True",
      ]
  - deploy staging: assert result.output == "deploying shop to staging in eu-west-1\n"
  - deploy production --help: assert "Deploy shop to production" in result.output
  - braces: assert "not a variable" in result.output

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Notable changes per release. Entries before 0.7.0 were reconstructed from the git history and tags, because no changelog was kept at the time; they list the main changes, not every commit. Release artifacts are on PyPI.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• cli ai llms-txt prints the documentation bundled with cliffy as one llms.txt file, for coding agents. It needs no model and no ai extra. The documentation site publishes the same file at /llms.txt. See AI commands.
  • cli validate warns when the default, help or short of a param is ignored because its type in types is a complete Typer definition.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • cli init accepts names with a hyphen, as cli init --raw always did.
The first release after a long pause. It brings the project up to date with current Python and dependency versions. Read the migration notes before upgrading.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Supported Python versions are now 3.11 to 3.15. Python 3.9 and 3.10 are no longer supported.
  • Depends on typer instead of typer-slim, so rich and shellingham are always installed.
  • Minimum dependency versions were raised to current releases, among them click>=8.2.1, typer>=0.24.0, pydantic>=2.12.0, rich-click>=1.9.0 and pydantic-ai>=2.0.0.
  • The ai extra requires pydantic-ai 2. Model names need a provider prefix. Without --model, the CLIFFY_AI_MODEL environment variable or a default for the provider whose API key is set is used, and generated manifests are validated before they are written. See AI commands.
  • cli build bundles the framework the generated code imports (Typer or rich-click), pinned to the installed version, writes a reproducible file and reports the Python version it needs.
  • Commands exit with 1 on failure, among them cli test when any test fails, cli build when a build fails and cli validate for an invalid manifest.
  • Include paths are looked up next to the including manifest first.
  • With the Click backend a bool option is a --flag/--no-flag switch, and short option names, global_params and cli test work as they do with Typer.
  • cli dev --run-cli is a real flag. It no longer re-runs the CLI on every reload when the flag is not given.
  • cli build prints the build output when a build fails.
  • Requires pybash 0.4. Shell lines are parsed like a shell parses them: quotes and backslashes reach the command unchanged, a value inserted into a > line is quoted, and > lines keep their quotes. See the migration notes.
  • A CLI imports pybash.runtime when it uses pipes, redirects or chains in $ lines, and nothing but subprocess otherwise. Built CLIs carry that helper themselves and do not need pybash.
  • A shell line that cannot be translated, or a Python syntax error in a script, is reported when the manifest is loaded, with the command, the line and the column.
  • After a build, cli build prints the size of the file and how to run it. --python has no fixed default any more: each target has its own.
  • The source distribution only contains the package, tests and examples.
  • Documentation: new site structure with a tutorial, task guides and reference pages generated from the code. Every manifest shown in the guides is run by make docs-check.
  • cli validate compiles and imports the generated code and reports a problem against the command it comes from. It used to check only the YAML, the schema and requires.
  • manifestVersion is checked. v1, v2 and unknown values stop the load with an error that says what to change, also in include files and blueprint specs. The key used to be ignored.
  • Click backend, explicit params: a name without -- is a positional argument, as it is with Typer. It used to become an option. Write name: --width for an option.
  • Click backend, shorthand arguments: label: str is optional and None when omitted, as it is with Typer. Write label: str! for a required argument.
  • Plain types in types are aliases for both backends. With Count: int, the param --n: Count is the option --n and an explicit param keeps its default and help. The Typer backend used to replace the whole definition, which made --n: Count a positional argument.
  • The Click backend supports types, command config (rich_help_panel becomes rich-click's panel), argument help, and Optional[...] and list[...] types. A Typer definition in a Click manifest is rejected with an error that names the command.
  • A manifest no code can be generated for (a command or param name that cannot be a Python name, an unknown template) stops every command with ~ error in <file>: command <name>: ... instead of a traceback.
  • Generated Click code imports rich-click when it is installed and plain Click otherwise, so use_click: true no longer needs the rich extra. cli build ships rich-click with such a CLI.
  • Generated code no longer starts with the time of generation. The first line is ## Generated <name> with cliffy <version>, so the same manifest renders the same code every time.
  • vars keys must be valid Python identifiers that the generated code does not use itself. my-var used to produce code that did not compile.
  • A var that refers to itself, or vars that refer to each other in a circle, are an error.
  • cli init --raw writes a manifest with one command and one test instead of an empty skeleton.
  • A corrupt metadata file is listed under the name of its CLI (hello, not hello.json), so it can be removed with cli rm.
  • make generate-clis renders examples/generated/ with scripts/examples.py and no longer installs packages. The generate-cleanup target is gone.
  • cli render prints exactly the generated module. Long lines are no longer broken, so cli render x.yaml > x.py is the code that runs. The # Rendered ... line goes to stderr. The same holds for cli init --render.
  • cli test reports errors against the manifest instead of printing tracebacks. A command that raises is shown as command <name> raised <Error>: <message> with the line of its run block; an assertion that raises or is not valid Python is shown with its line; a manifest that does not import and a shell step that cannot be started end the run with an error message.
  • cli remove removes a CLI completely or not at all. When the launcher is not the file cliffy wrote, nothing is removed, the CLI stays loaded and the command exits with 1. cli remove-all exits with 1 when a CLI could not be removed.
  • cli load only replaces a launcher it wrote itself: a regular file with exactly the launcher text for that CLI. A file that merely contained from cliffy.clis. used to count as cliffy's own.
  • A requires entry that starts with - is rejected. requires lists packages.
  • cli dev runs one reload at a time. A second save within a second of the first is no longer dropped.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• cli build --target chooses what is built from the same manifest: zipapp (the default, as before), script for a single Python file with its dependencies declared inline, to run with uv, and native for a compiled executable that brings its own Python. See Building executables.
  • Shell lines support &&, ||, ;, |&, 2>, &>, 2>&1, $(command), continuation lines and comments. See Shell commands.
  • Blueprints: custom YAML specs that map onto a CLI, selected with --blueprint or a blueprint: key, and the cli blueprint list and cli blueprint schema commands.
  • callbacks in manifests: code that runs before the commands of the CLI or of a group, for both backends.
  • vars values can be numbers and booleans, and a var can be built from other vars in any order.
  • cli dev also watches included manifests and the Python file of a file blueprint.
  • The manifest's examples are shown at the end of the --help of the generated CLI, for both backends. See Generating docs.
  • cli test --traceback prints the full Python traceback of a command that raises.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Text from a manifest (help, names, defaults, versions) is escaped in the generated code and names are validated, so manifest data cannot change the code that is generated.
  • The name given to cli remove, update, info, build and docs is validated. A name such as ../x could select and delete files outside of cliffy's own directories.
  • Launchers and generated modules are written to a temporary file and renamed into place, a new launcher is only created when nothing has its name, and symbolic links are never followed.
  • cli build never passes a requires entry to pip as an option. An entry such as --index-url=... used to change where pip installs from.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • The cliffy[dev] extra. Development dependencies are a dependency group (uv sync).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Manifest file handles are closed after cli update and after loading a manifest.
  • cli --version prints cliffy's version. With the rich extra it printed the version of rich-click.
  • Line breaks in command and group help become spaces (Greet\nuser was shown as Greetuser) and blank lines stay paragraph breaks.
  • Two manifest names that map to the same Python name (command db-app and group db, a command and a name from imports, functions or vars) no longer break the generated module.
  • The cli test counter counts test cases only; it could print 10 of 9.
  • cli test removes colors and styles from the output before the assertions run. On a CI system rich styles help output, which made tests that passed locally fail there.
  • A Jinja error in a manifest is reported with file, line and the text of the line instead of a traceback.
  • The field descriptions in the JSON schema and the cli init template were wrong in places.
  • cli dev: a reload that started earlier can no longer finish last and load an older version of the manifest over a newer one.
  • cli dev --run-cli and cli test on several threads no longer delete each other's temporary files. Each run has a temporary directory of its own.
  • The MCP example blueprint answers a JSON-RPC message that is not an object, or a batch, with an error instead of exiting.
  • Releases: the upload to PyPI can be re-run after it stopped half way.
  • cliffy type-checks and its test suite passes without the optional extras. The test suite no longer extracts zipapps into ~/.shiv.
  • Compatibility with Click 8.2 and later, rich-click 1.9 and Python 3.12 and later (deprecated APIs replaced).

• Changed the default model of the AI commands.
  • Documentation updates.

• Added the cli ai generate and cli ai ask commands behind the new ai extra.
  • Added cli docs to generate Markdown, reStructuredText or HTML documentation for a CLI, and the examples manifest key that feeds it.
  • Expanded the documentation site.

• Added the Click backend (use_click: true) and refactored code generation into per-framework commanders.
  • Moved the project to uv.
  • Added Python 3.13 to the test matrix and extended the test suite.
• Reworked command parameter parsing.
• Added the todo example and documentation updates.

• Manifest schema v3. args was renamed to params; v2 manifests are rejected.
  • Added global_params.
  • Added the JSON schema for manifests and cli init --json-schema.

• Manifest schema v2; v1 manifests are rejected.
  • Added command templates and the pre_run and post_run hooks.
  • First version of the documentation site.

• Added cli test and the tests manifest key.
  • Added Python 3.12 to the test matrix.
  • Fixed path handling on Windows.
• Added command aliases.
• Added cli dev (hot reload) and cli rm-all.
• Declared Click as an explicit dependency.
• CLI metadata is stored inside the installed package.

• Merged the bundle command into cli build.
  • Type-checking fixes.

docs.title: 0.3.0 to 0.3.2 (2023-06)
docs.text: • Internal refactoring and a newer pybash.
• Environment variables can be used in vars.

• Added cli run.
  • Executables are built with shiv.

• Rich became optional.
  • Windows fixes.
• Added requires.

• Added vars with Jinja2 templating.
  • Added includes with deep merging.
• Added loading, unloading and listing of CLIs.

• Added cli init.
  • Several manifests can be loaded in one call.
  • Added manifest versioning.

docs.title: 0.2.0 and 0.2.1 (2023-03-09)
docs.text:
• Renamed the project to cliffy.
  • Added help, cli_options, option aliases, custom imports and a shorter param syntax.
• First release.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Bug reports, fixes and documentation improvements are welcome. Open an issue or a pull request on GitHub.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
You need uv and one of the supported Python versions (3.11 to 3.15).

$ git clone https://github.com/jaykv/cliffy.git
$ cd cliffy
$ make install        # uv sync --frozen --all-extras --group docs
$ uv run cli --help

make install creates .venv with cliffy in editable mode, both extras, the test tools and the documentation tools. To work on another Python version, run uv sync --all-extras --python 3.15.

On macOS with Python 3.14 or 3.15, some dependencies are built from source, which needs the Xcode command line tools.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
Command What it does make test Runs the test suite in parallel with coverage. make lint Checks formatting and lint rules with ruff, then types with mypy. make format Formats the code and applies ruff's automatic fixes. make check format, lint, test and clean in one go. make docs-serve Serves the documentation at http://127.0.0.1:8000 with live reload. make docs-generate Regenerates the reference pages. make docs-check Checks the reference pages and runs every documentation manifest. make docs-build docs-check, then a strict documentation build. make generate-schema Regenerates examples/cliffy_schema.json from the models. make generate-clis Regenerates examples/generated/*.py from the manifests in examples/. make clean Removes build and cache directories.

Run a single test file or test with pytest directly:

$ uv run pytest tests/test_manifest.py -v
$ uv run pytest tests/test_manifest.py::test_validate_cli_requires -v

Run the tests through uv run so that the environment's bin directory is on the PATH; tests that load CLIs start them by name. Do not run two test sessions in the same checkout at once, because loaded CLIs are shared state.

CI runs make lint and make test on Python 3.11 to 3.15 for every pull request.

docs.title: How the code is organized
docs.text:
A manifest goes through three stages:

YAML file ─► Transformer ─► CLIManifest ─► Commander ─► Python source ─► Loader / builder
Module Role cliffy/transformer.py Renders the manifest with Jinja2, resolves includes, validates it and checks requires. cliffy/manifest.py The pydantic models that define the manifest format and the JSON schema. cliffy/commander.py Builds groups, merges command templates and drives code generation. cliffy/commanders/typer.py, click.py Emit Typer or Click code. cliffy/parser.py Translates params and run scripts for the Typer backend. cliffy/cli.py, cliffy/ai.py The cli command itself. cliffy/loader.py, cliffy/homer.py Install generated CLIs and keep their metadata. cliffy/builder.py cli run and cli build. cliffy/reloader.py cli dev. cliffy/tester.py cli test. cliffy/doc.py cli docs.

When you add a manifest key, update the model in cliffy/manifest.py, handle it in the commanders, then run make generate-schema and make docs-generate.

docs.title: Working on the documentation
docs.text: The site is built with MkDocs Material from the docs/ directory. The build is strict: a broken link or a missing file is an error.

docs.title: Generated pages
docs.text:
Three pages are written by scripts/docs.py and must not be edited by hand:

Page Generated from docs/reference/cli.md The Click commands in cliffy/cli.py and cliffy/ai.py docs/reference/manifest.md The models in cliffy/manifest.py docs/reference/examples.md The manifests in examples/

After changing a command, an option, a model or an example, run make docs-generate and commit the result. The hand-written notes on those pages live in scripts/docs.py, next to the code that renders them. The script stops with a message when a new command, argument, model field or example has no description yet.

docs.title: Manifests in the guides
docs.text:
Guides do not contain copies of YAML. They embed files from docs/snippets/ (or examples/) with the snippet syntax, optionally limited to a named section:

--8<-- "docs/snippets/params.yaml:shorthand"

A section is the part of the YAML file between a pair of marker comments that carry its name. Open any file in docs/snippets/ to see them; the snippets extension documents the syntax.

Every manifest in docs/snippets/ should have a tests section. make docs-check loads each one, compiles the generated code and runs its tests, so a guide cannot show a manifest that does not work. When you add console output to a page, copy it from a real run.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text: $ make docs-serve

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
1. Set the version in pyproject.toml and run uv lock.
  2. Move the "unreleased" entry in docs/project/changelog.md under the new version and date, and add migration notes for breaking changes.
  3. Merge to main, then publish a GitHub release whose tag equals the version (0.7.0 or v0.7.0).

The publish.yaml workflow builds the package, checks that the tag matches the version and uploads to PyPI through trusted publishing. Pushing documentation changes to main deploys the site.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: Behavior in cliffy 0.7.1 that differs from what you might expect, with the way around each. Every item was reproduced against this release. The guides already recommend the forms that work; this page explains why.

docs.title: Some problems are only found by cli validate and cli test
docs.text:
Every command checks the scripts of a manifest and reports a syntax error with its command, line and column. A problem that only shows when the generated code is imported is not found by cli load, cli render or cli build: a type name that does not exist, or params that do not fit together in one signature. The CLI is then loaded or built and fails when it is started.

Do this instead: run cli validate first. It imports the generated code and reports such a problem against the command it comes from.

docs.title: cli test does not check shell steps
docs.text: A $ or > step that exits with an error does not fail the run. A step whose program does not exist ends the run with an error message. See Testing manifests.

docs.title: Examples are shown for the CLI, not per command
docs.text: examples belongs to the manifest. The generated CLI shows all of them at the end of its own --help; the help of a single command has no examples section, because a command has no examples key. With the Typer backend an example that contains an emoji code such as :rocket: is shown as the emoji, like the rest of the help text.

docs.title: cli remove refuses when the launcher was changed
docs.text:
The launcher of a loaded CLI is only deleted while it is exactly the file cliffy wrote. After an edit, or when another program replaced it, cli remove and cli remove-all remove nothing for that CLI and exit with 1.

Do this instead: move or delete the file named in the message, then run cli remove again.

docs.title: A file can still appear between cliffy's check and its write
docs.text: cliffy checks a launcher right before it replaces or deletes it, never follows a symbolic link and creates a new launcher only when nothing has the name. Replacing or deleting an existing launcher is a check followed by a rename or an unlink: a file that another process puts at exactly that path in between is replaced or removed. This needs write access to the environment's bin directory at that moment.

docs.title: Includes fall back to the working directory
docs.text:
An include path is looked up next to the including manifest first. When it is not found there, it is looked up in the directory cli is run from, so the same manifest can pick up a different file depending on where you are.

Do this instead: keep include files next to (or below) the manifest that lists them.

docs.title: A full Typer definition in types replaces the param's own settings
docs.text: A types entry with typer.Option(...) or typer.Argument(...) is the complete definition. A default, help or short written on a param that uses it is ignored, and cli validate warns about it. Plain types such as Count: int do not have this effect. See Params and types.

docs.title: Click backend
docs.text: use_click: true supports every manifest feature. Generic params and full definitions in types are written as Click decorators instead of Typer expressions. The details are in Click and Typer backends.

docs.title: Migration notes
docs.text: What to change when you upgrade. Each section lists the breaking changes of one release and the action to take. The full list of changes is in the changelog.

docs.title: Python 3.11 or newer is required
docs.text:
cliffy 0.7.0 supports Python 3.11 to 3.15. On Python 3.9 or 3.10, pip keeps installing 0.6.1.

Action: upgrade the interpreter of the environment cliffy is installed in, then reinstall:

$ python --version
$ pip install --upgrade cliffy

Loaded CLIs are tied to an environment. After moving to a new environment, load your manifests again with cli load.

docs.title: typer replaces typer-slim
docs.text:
cliffy now depends on the full typer package, which always installs rich and shellingham. Generated CLIs therefore always have Rich-formatted help.

Action: none in most cases. If you pinned typer-slim next to cliffy in a requirements file, replace it with typer.

docs.title: The dev extra is gone
docs.text:
pip install "cliffy[dev]" no longer exists.

Action: contributors set up the project with uv sync --all-extras. See Contributing.

docs.title: AI commands: model names need a provider
docs.text:
The ai extra now requires pydantic-ai 2, which only accepts model names in provider:model form.

Before Now --model gpt-4o --model openai:gpt-4o --model gemini-2.0-flash --model google:gemini-2.0-flash

Action: add the provider prefix wherever you pass --model or -m. The default model is google:gemini-2.0-flash.

docs.title: cli dev --run-cli
docs.text:
In 0.6.x with Click 8.2 or later, the CLI was run after every reload even without --run-cli. Now it only runs when the flag is given.

Action: add --run-cli to your cli dev command if you relied on the old behavior.

docs.title: Shell lines follow shell quoting
docs.text:
cliffy 0.7.0 uses pybash 0.4, which parses $ lines the way a shell does. Most lines behave as before. These changed:

Line Before Now $ echo 'a\nb' Python read the backslash: two lines of output The command gets a\nb, as in a shell > echo f{name} The value was pasted into the shell command The value is quoted and is always one word > grep "two words" file The quotes were removed before the shell saw them The shell gets the line as written out = $ ls \| wc -l out was a process object out is the output of the pipeline, as bytes $ echo a > one.txt > two.txt The second file got a copy of the first Both files get the output $ make && echo ok NotImplementedError Runs echo ok when make succeeds

Action: run cli test on your manifests. If a > line relied on a value being pasted in as shell syntax, for example a glob pattern, see When you need a real shell.

A script that is not valid Python, or a $ line that cannot be translated, now stops cli load with a message that names the command and the line. Before, the CLI was generated and failed when it ran.

docs.title: cli build output
docs.text: cli build prints two more things after a build, the size of the file and how to run it. Scripts that read that output need to be adjusted. The file itself is built as before; the new --target option is described in Building executables.

docs.title: Manifests
docs.text:
The manifest format is still schema v3, and most manifests written for 0.5.x and 0.6.x load without changes, apart from the shell lines described above. A few things that used to be accepted silently are now checked, and the Click backend follows the documented meaning of params.

What Before Now Action manifestVersion: v1 or v2 Ignored An error Set manifestVersion: v3 or remove the line. A vars key such as my-var, cli or class Generated code that did not compile An error Rename the var, for example to my_var. A var that refers to itself Left as literal {{ }} text An error Remove the reference, or wrap literal braces in {% raw %}. types: {Count: int} with --n: Count (Typer) The positional argument n The option --n None if you meant an option. For an argument, write n: Count. types: {Count: int = 1} with n: Count (Typer) The option --n An optional argument Write --n: Count for an option. use_click: explicit param name: width The option --width A positional argument Write name: --width. use_click: shorthand name: str A required argument An optional argument, None when omitted Write name: str!. use_click: config on a command Ignored Applied Remove settings you did not mean, such as hidden: true. use_click: a typer.Option(...) definition Copied into code that failed at run time An error when the manifest is loaded Write a Click decorator, see Click and Typer backends. First line of the generated code ## Generated <name> on <time> ## Generated <name> with cliffy <version> None, unless a script of yours reads that line.

Run cli validate on each manifest after upgrading. It now also compiles and imports the generated code.

docs.title: From 0.4.x to 0.5.0 (schema v3)
docs.text:
The main change is that args on a command was renamed to params.

Action: rename the key in every command, and set manifestVersion: v3 or remove the line. Then run cli validate on the manifest to find anything else the schema no longer accepts.

docs.title: From 0.3.x to 0.4.0 (schema v2)
docs.text:
Manifests written for 0.3.x use the v1 format, which later releases do not read.

Action: rewrite the manifest in the current format. The Quickstart and the manifest reference describe it, and cli init mycli --raw writes a minimal manifest to start from.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
Installing cliffy adds two identical entry points, cli and cliffy. This page uses cli. It is generated from the command definitions in cliffy/cli.py and cliffy/ai.py, so the arguments, options and defaults below are the ones the installed version accepts.

cli [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

docs.title: Commands at a glance
docs.text: Command Description cli ai AI-powered commands. generate and ask require the ai extra: pip install 'cliffy[ai]' cli blueprint Work with blueprints: custom YAML specs that map onto a CLI cli build Build a CLI manifest or a loaded CLI into a single file to hand to someone else cli dev Start hot-reloader for a manifest for active development. cli docs Generate documentation for a CLI cli info Display CLI info cli init Generate a CLI manifest template cli list List all CLIs loaded cli load Load CLI for given manifest(s) cli remove Remove a loaded CLI by name cli remove-all Remove all loaded CLIs cli render Render the CLI manifest generation as code cli run Run CLI for a manifest cli test Run tests defined in a manifest cli update Reloads CLI by name cli validate Validate a CLI manifest: its structure, its requirements and the code generated from it

docs.title: Global options
docs.text: Option Description --version Print the version and exit. --aliases List the command aliases and exit. -h, --help Show help. Every command accepts this option.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Aliases are hidden from cli --help. cli --aliases prints this list.

Alias Command cli ls cli list cli add cli load cli reload cli update cli rm cli remove cli rm-all cli remove-all cli rmall cli remove-all cli blueprints cli blueprint list

docs.title: cli ai
docs.text:
AI-powered commands. generate and ask require the ai extra: pip install 'cliffy[ai]'

cli ai [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

generate and ask need the ai extra (pip install "cliffy[ai]"). Both send the manifest JSON schema to the model as part of the prompt and print token usage when they finish. llms-txt needs no extra and calls no model.

Model names use the pydantic-ai provider:model form, and the API key of that provider must be set in the environment. Without --model, the CLIFFY_AI_MODEL environment variable is used, then a default for the first provider that has an API key set. See AI commands.

docs.title: cli ai ask
docs.text:
Ask a question about cliffy or a specific CLI manifest.

cli ai ask [OPTIONS] PROMPT
Argument or option Type Required Default Description PROMPT text yes Your question. --preview flag no Print the prompt instead of sending it. Needs no model. --max-tokens integer range no Maximum number of tokens in a model response. -m, --model text no Model to use, as provider:model. See https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/overview/. Defaults to a model of the first provider with an API key set, else google:gemini-flash-latest. --cli file no Loaded CLI or manifest to include in the prompt as reference.

--preview prints the prompt and exits without calling a model.

docs.title: cli ai generate
docs.text:
Generate a CLI manifest based on a description.

cli ai generate [OPTIONS] CLI_NAME DESCRIPTION
Argument or option Type Required Default Description CLI_NAME text yes Name of the CLI. The manifest is written to <cli_name>.yaml. DESCRIPTION text yes Plain-language description of the CLI you want. --preview flag no Print the prompt instead of sending it. Needs no model. --max-tokens integer range no Maximum number of tokens in a model response. -m, --model text no Model to use, as provider:model. See https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/overview/. Defaults to a model of the first provider with an API key set, else google:gemini-flash-latest. --retries integer range no 2 How often to send an invalid manifest back to the model to be fixed. -f, --force flag no Overwrite the manifest file if it exists. -o, --output-dir directory no . Output directory

The reply of the model is validated before the manifest is written, and sent back with the reason when it is not a manifest cliffy can load. --preview prints the prompt and exits without calling a model.

docs.title: cli ai llms-txt
docs.text:
Print the bundled cliffy documentation as llms.txt. Needs no model.

cli ai llms-txt [OPTIONS]

Prints the documentation that is bundled with the installed cliffy as one text file, in the llms.txt layout. It needs no model, no API key and no ai extra, so it works offline and always matches the installed version.

$ cli ai llms-txt > cliffy-llms.txt
$ cli ai llms-txt | pbcopy

Give the output to a coding agent, or add it to a project's context, so that it can write manifests without looking anything up.

docs.title: cli blueprint
docs.text:
Work with blueprints: custom YAML specs that map onto a CLI

cli blueprint [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

A blueprint lets a YAML file use its own keys instead of commands and params, and maps them onto a CLI. See Blueprints.

docs.title: cli blueprint list
docs.text:
List the blueprints provided by installed packages

cli blueprint list [OPTIONS]

Alias: cli blueprints

Lists the blueprints that installed packages register under the cliffy.blueprints entry point group. A blueprint in a .py file or referenced as module:Class works without being listed.

$ cli blueprint list
No blueprints installed. Use a .py file or module:Class reference, or install a blueprint package.

docs.title: cli blueprint schema
docs.text:
Print the JSON schema of a blueprint's spec, for validation and editor completion

cli blueprint schema [OPTIONS] BLUEPRINT
Argument or option Type Required Default Description BLUEPRINT text yes Blueprint reference: a .py file, module:Class or the name of an installed blueprint. -o, --output file no Write the schema to a file 
$ cli blueprint schema examples/blueprints/tasks.py -o tasks.schema.json
+ tasks.schema.json

Point a # yaml-language-server: $schema= comment at the file to get completion and validation for files written in the blueprint's spec.

docs.title: cli build
docs.text:
Build a CLI manifest or a loaded CLI into a single file to hand to someone else

cli build [OPTIONS] [CLI_OR_MANIFESTS]...
Argument or option Type Required Default Description [CLI_OR_MANIFESTS]... file no Manifest files (paths ending in yaml) or names of loaded CLIs. -t, --target zipapp | script | native no zipapp What to build: zipapp is a zipapp with its dependencies bundled, which needs a compatible Python; script is a .py script that declares its dependencies inline, which needs uv or an environment with them; native is a compiled executable that brings its own Python and needs nothing installed (built with cargo and uv). -o, --output-dir directory no Output dir -p, --python text no Interpreter for the #! line of a zipapp or a script, added after the #!. [default: /usr/bin/env python3 for a zipapp, /usr/bin/env -S uv run --script for a script] -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Builds one file to hand to someone else. --target chooses what kind:

Target What you get Needs on the other machine zipapp hello, a zipapp built with shiv that contains the dependencies A compatible Python script hello.py, a script with its dependencies declared inline uv, or Python with the dependencies installed native hello, a compiled executable with its own Python Nothing

Every target ships the generated CLI, the framework it imports (Typer, or rich-click with use_click) and every package listed under requires. Without --output-dir the file is written to the current directory.

$ cli build hello.yaml -o dist
+ hello built 📦
  dist/hello (single file, needs Python >=3.10, 1.8 MB)
  run it with: ./dist/hello
$ ./dist/hello greet Ada
Hello, Ada!
$ cli build hello.yaml -o dist --target script
+ hello built 📦
  dist/hello.py (single file, needs uv, or Python >=3.11 with typer==0.27.3 installed, 1.3 kB)
  run it with: ./dist/hello.py (or: uv run dist/hello.py)
  uv downloads the dependencies the first time the script runs

The native target needs cargo and uv on the machine that builds. When a build fails, the reason is printed and the exit code is 1. With --blueprint, or a blueprint: key in the file, the blueprint is applied at build time and is not needed to run the result.

See Building executables.

docs.title: cli dev
docs.text:
Start hot-reloader for a manifest for active development.

Examples:

  • cli dev examples/hello.yaml

  • cli dev examples/hello.yaml --run-cli -- -h

  • cli dev examples/hello.yaml --run-cli python

cli dev [OPTIONS] MANIFEST [RUN_CLI_ARGS]...
Argument or option Type Required Default Description MANIFEST file yes Manifest file to watch. [RUN_CLI_ARGS]... text no Arguments for the generated CLI when --run-cli is set. --run-cli flag no If passed, runs CLI on each reload. Useful for syntax checks or testing command execution on each reload -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Nothing is loaded when the command starts. The CLI is loaded the first time the file changes and again on every later change. The manifests it includes and the Python file of its blueprint are watched too. Stop with Ctrl+C.

With --run-cli, the remaining arguments are passed to the freshly generated CLI after each reload. Put -- before them when they include options.

See Hot-reload dev loop.

docs.title: cli docs
docs.text:
Generate documentation for a CLI

cli docs [OPTIONS] CLI_OR_MANIFEST
Argument or option Type Required Default Description CLI_OR_MANIFEST file yes Manifest file (a path ending in yaml) or the name of a loaded CLI. -f, --format md | rst | html no md Output format. -o, --output-dir directory no Output directory -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Writes <name>.md, <name>.rst or <name>.html to the output directory, or to the current directory when --output-dir is not given. The output directory must exist.

A loaded CLI is documented from the manifest path recorded by cli load.

See Generating docs.

docs.title: cli info
docs.text:
Display CLI info

cli info [OPTIONS] CLI_NAME
Argument or option Type Required Default Description CLI_NAME text yes Name of a loaded CLI.

Prints the name, version, requirements, blueprint (when one was used), age and stored manifest of a loaded CLI.

docs.title: cli init
docs.text:
Generate a CLI manifest template

cli init [OPTIONS] [CLI_NAME]
Argument or option Type Required Default Description [CLI_NAME] text no mycli Name of the CLI. The manifest is written to <cli_name>.yaml. --render flag no Print template to terminal directly --raw flag no Raw template without boilerplate helpers and examples. --json-schema flag no Write JSON schema (cliffy_schema.json) file to the current directory. Useful for development. 
$ cli init mycli --raw
+ mycli.yaml

--raw writes a skeleton with every top-level key, one hello command and one test. Without --raw the manifest is a commented tour of the format with example commands. Both run and pass cli test as written.

--json-schema also writes cliffy_schema.json and adds a # yaml-language-server comment that points at it. See Editor setup.

docs.title: cli load
docs.text:
Load CLI for given manifest(s)

cli load [OPTIONS] [MANIFESTS]...

Alias: cli add

Argument or option Type Required Default Description [MANIFESTS]... file no One or more manifest files to load. -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Loading does three things:

  1. generates the CLI code and writes it to cliffy/clis/<name>.py inside the installed cliffy package,
  2. writes a launcher script called <name> into the bin directory of the Python environment cliffy is installed in,
  3. records the manifest path and contents so that cli list, cli info and cli update can find it.

The CLI is therefore available wherever that environment is active. Packages listed under requires must already be installed, otherwise loading stops with missing requirement.

A file written in a blueprint's spec is loaded the same way. The blueprint comes from --blueprint or from the file's blueprint: key and is remembered, so cli update applies it again.

$ cli load hello.yaml
✨ Generated hello CLI v0.1.0 ✨
$ hello -h

See Hot-reload dev loop.

docs.title: cli remove
docs.text:
Remove a loaded CLI by name

cli remove [OPTIONS] [CLI_NAMES]...

Alias: cli rm

Argument or option Type Required Default Description [CLI_NAMES]... text no Names of loaded CLIs to remove.

Deletes the launcher script, the generated module and the stored metadata.

$ cli remove hello
~ hello removed 💥

docs.title: cli remove-all
docs.text:
Remove all loaded CLIs

cli remove-all [OPTIONS]

Aliases: cli rm-all, cli rmall

docs.title: cli render
docs.text:
Render the CLI manifest generation as code

cli render [OPTIONS] MANIFEST
Argument or option Type Required Default Description MANIFEST file yes Manifest file to render. -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Prints the Python module cliffy generates, without loading or running it. Use it to see exactly how params, shell lines and templates are translated.

$ cli render hello.yaml

docs.title: cli run
docs.text:
Run CLI for a manifest

cli run [OPTIONS] MANIFEST [CLI_ARGS]...
Argument or option Type Required Default Description MANIFEST file yes Manifest file to run. [CLI_ARGS]... text no Arguments passed to the generated CLI. Put -- first when they include options. -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Generates the CLI in a temporary file and runs it once, without loading it. Options meant for your CLI must come after --, otherwise cli run tries to parse them itself:

$ cli run hello.yaml greet Ada
Hello, Ada!
$ cli run hello.yaml -- greet Ada --shout
HELLO, ADA!
$ cli run hello.yaml -- --help

Help output shows the temporary file name instead of the CLI name.

docs.title: cli test
docs.text:
Run tests defined in a manifest

cli test [OPTIONS] MANIFEST
Argument or option Type Required Default Description MANIFEST file yes Manifest file whose tests section should run. -x, --exitfirst flag no exit instantly on first error or failed test. --traceback flag no Also print the full Python traceback of a command that raises. -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Runs the tests section of a manifest and prints each command, its output and the result. The exit code is 0 only when every test passes. It is 1 when a test fails or when the manifest has no tests.

See Testing manifests.

docs.title: cli update
docs.text:
Reloads CLI by name

cli update [OPTIONS] [CLI_NAMES]...

Alias: cli reload

Argument or option Type Required Default Description [CLI_NAMES]... text no Names of loaded CLIs to regenerate from their manifests.

update re-reads the manifest from the path recorded by cli load, so it only works while the manifest is still at that location.

$ cli update hello
✨ Reloaded hello CLI v0.1.0 ✨
$ hello -h

docs.title: cli validate
docs.text:
Validate a CLI manifest: its structure, its requirements and the code generated from it

cli validate [OPTIONS] MANIFEST
Argument or option Type Required Default Description MANIFEST file yes Manifest file to validate. -b, --blueprint text no Blueprint that maps a custom YAML spec onto a CLI: a .py file, module:Class or an installed blueprint name. Overrides the blueprint: key of the file.

Checks that the file is valid YAML, matches the manifest schema, that its requires are installed and that the generated code works. Scripts are checked while the code is generated, as they are by every other command. validate then compiles and imports the generated code, which defines the commands without running any of them. The code in imports and functions and the expressions in vars do run.

$ cli validate hello.yaml
Manifest hello.yaml is valid

An error in a script is reported with its command, line and column. A problem that only shows when the code is imported, such as a type that does not exist, is reported against the command it comes from:

$ cli validate broken.yaml
~ error in broken.yaml: command `db.create`, run, line 2, column 7: not valid Python: '(' was never closed
    print((
          ^ 💔
$ cli validate other.yaml
Manifest other.yaml is invalid: the generated code does not work
  command `db.create`: NameError: name 'Table' is not defined
    def db_create(table: Table = typer.Argument(...)): 💔

docs.title: hello
docs.text:
The smallest useful manifest: one shell command, one Python command and a tests section.

$ cli run examples/hello.yaml python
examples/hello.yaml 
# yaml-language-server: $schema=cliffy_schema.json

name: hello
version: 0.1.0
help: Hello world!

commands:
  shell: $echo "hello from shell"
  python: print("hello from python")

examples:
  - command: hello shell
    description: Say hello from a shell command.
  - command: hello python
    description: Say hello from Python.

tests:
  - shell: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - python: assert result.output == "hello from python\n"
  - shell --help: assert "Show this message and exit" in result.output
  - -h: assert "Hello world!" in result.output
  - -h: assert "Examples:" in result.output and "$ hello shell" in result.output

docs.title: town
docs.text:
A larger CLI: groups with help text, shared types, short option aliases, command aliases and a (*).list command that is added to every group.

$ cli run examples/town.yaml land list
examples/town.yaml 
# yaml-language-server: $schema=cliffy_schema.json

manifestVersion: v3 # optional (default is the latest)
name: town
version: 0.1.1

imports: |
  import re
  import time

functions:
  - |
    def format_money(money: float):
        return "${:.2f}".format(money)

commands:
  people:
    help: Manage people
  shops:
    help: Manage shops
  home:
    help: Manage homes
  land:
    help: Manage land
  land.build:
    params: [name: Name!, address: str!, --value|-v: int = 100]
    run: |
      """Build land"""
      print(f"building land {name}")
  land.sell:
    params: [name: Name!, money: Money]
    run: |
      """Sell land"""
      print(f"selling land {name}")
  land.buy:
    params: [name: Name!, money: Money]
    run: |
      """Buy land"""
      print(f"buying land {name} for {format_money(money)}")
  people.add:
    params: [fullname: str!, age: int!, --home|-h: str]
    run: |
      """Add a person to town"""
      print(f"adding person {fullname}, {age}, {home}")
  people.remove:
    params: [fullname: str!]
    run: |
      """Remove person from town"""
      print(f"removing person {fullname}")
  shops.build:
    params: [name: Name!, land: str!, --type|-t: str]
    run: |
      """Build a shop"""
      print(f"building shop {name} ({type}) on land {land}")
  shops.sell:
    params: [name: Name!, money: Money]
    run: |
      """Sell a shop"""
      print(f"selling shop {name} for ${money}")
  shops.buy:
    params: [name: Name!, money: Money]
    run: |
      """Buy a shop"""
      print(f"buying shop {name} for ${money}")
  home.build|bu:
    params: [address: str!, land: str, owner: str]
    run: |
      """Build a home"""
      print(f"building home at {address} for {owner} on land {land}")
  home.sell:
    params: [address: str!, money: Money]
    aliases: ["s"]
    run: |
      """Sell a home"""
      print(f"selling home {address} for {format_money(money)}")
  home.buy:
    params: [address: str!, money: Money]
    aliases: ["b"]
    run: |
      """Buy a home"""
      print(f"buying home {address} for {money}")
  (*).list:
    params: [--limit|-l: int]
    run: |
      """Get a list of {(*)}"""
      print(f"listing {(*)}")

types:
  Money: float = typer.Option(..., help="Amount of money", min=0)
  Name: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Name")

docs.title: template
docs.text:
A command template that gives two commands the same params, a run script written as a list, and per-command config.

$ cli run examples/template.yaml -- debug one --local-arg-2 two
examples/template.yaml 
# yaml-language-server: $schema=cliffy_schema.json

name: template
version: 0.1.0

vars:
  GLOBAL_VAR: hello

command_templates:
  common_params:
    params:
      - local_arg: str!
      - --local_arg_2: str = ""

commands:
  hello:
    help: |
      Demo. global var and command args usage. 
      Runs hello command by default based on GLOBAL_VAR.
    template: common_params
    run:
      - $ echo "{{GLOBAL_VAR}} f{local_arg} --f{local_arg_2}"
    config:
      deprecated: True
      context_settings:
        help_option_names: ["-h", "--helpme"]
